questions.name: D016 — Cardiology · Prosthetic heart valves
questions.questionStem: What is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 28-year-old man presents to the Acute Medical Unit with a two-day history of sharp central chest pain, worse on deep inspiration and relieved by leaning forward.

🩺 Examination:

He is afebrile and haemodynamically stable.

🔬 Investigations:

An ECG shows 2mm ST elevation in leads I, II, aVF, and V2-V6, with PR depression in lead II. A transthoracic echocardiogram reveals a trivial pericardial effusion with normal ventricular function.

Hb 148 g/L (135-180)

Platelets 250 x 109/L (150 - 400)

WBC 11.2 x 109/L (4.0 - 11.0)

Creatinine 80 µmol/L (55 - 120)

CRP 78 mg/L (< 5)

Troponin T 95 ng/L (< 14)

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
The clinical presentation, with sharp, pleuritic, and positional chest pain, is classic for acute pericarditis. The ECG confirms this diagnosis, showing widespread ST elevation and PR depression. The raised troponin suggests an element of myocardial inflammation (myopericarditis), which is a common finding and does not change the initial management in a haemodynamically stable patient. The raised CRP is also consistent with inflammation.

Ibuprofen and colchicine is the correct answer. Current UK and European guidelines recommend combination therapy with a non- steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) and colchicine as first-line treatment for acute idiopathic or viral pericarditis. This approach has been shown to be superior to NSAID monotherapy in resolving symptoms and, crucially, in reducing the rate of recurrent or incessant pericarditis. Treatment is typically continued for 1-2 weeks until symptoms resolve and CRP normalises, after which the NSAID is tapered. Colchicine is usually continued for three months to prevent recurrence.

  • ❌ Aspirin and clopidogrel would be the appropriate management for an acute coronary syndrome (ACS). While the ST elevation and raised troponin make ACS a key differential, the clinical features are much more suggestive of pericarditis. The pain is pleuritic and positional, and the ECG changes are widespread (not conforming to a coronary artery territory) and accompanied by PR depression, which is highly specific for pericarditis. Initiating dual antiplatelet therapy would be inappropriate and could increase the risk of a haemorrhagic pericardial effusion.
  • ❌ Colchicine alone is not the standard first-line therapy. While colchicine is a vital component of treatment for preventing recurrence, NSAIDs are more effective for rapid control of pain and inflammation in the acute phase. Colchicine monotherapy might be considered in a patient with a strong contraindication to NSAIDs, but it is not the preferred initial strategy for most patients. The combination is superior.
  • ❌ Ibuprofen alone was previously the standard of care but is now considered suboptimal. Multiple trials have demonstrated that adding colchicine to an NSAID significantly reduces the risk of treatment failure and recurrence of pericarditis. While an NSAID alone will provide symptomatic relief for many patients, it is no longer recommended as first-line monotherapy due to the proven benefits of combination treatment.
  • ❌ Prednisolone is generally reserved as a second or third-line agent for acute pericarditis. Corticosteroids are used for patients who have contraindications to or have failed to respond to NSAIDs and colchicine, or for specific underlying causes such as autoimmune disease or post- pericardiotomy syndrome. Early use of corticosteroids is actively discouraged in idiopathic/viral pericarditis as it is associated with a higher risk of chronic and recurrent disease.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Mechanical valves require a vitamin K antagonist. DOACs are contraindicated — they were inferior in trial and carry excess thrombosis and bleeding in this setting.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D017 — Cardiology · Pulmonary arterial hypertension
questions.questionStem: What is the usual target INR for a patient with a mechanical mitral valve?
questions.explanationHtml:
For a patient with a mechanical mitral valve, the correct target INR is 3.5. This higher target INR is necessary because mechanical mitral valves carry a greater risk of thromboembolism compared to mechanical aortic valves. The mitral position experiences lower pressure and flow conditions which increases the risk of thrombus formation. Current guidelines recommend maintaining an INR between 3.0-4.0 for mechanical mitral valves, with a target of 3.5.

  • ❌ 2.0 is too low for any mechanical valve and would place the patient at significant risk of valve thrombosis and systemic embolism. This target would be more appropriate for conditions like atrial fibrillation.
  • ❌ 2.5 is also insufficient for a mechanical mitral valve. While this might be an appropriate target for a mechanical aortic valve (target range 2.0-3.0), it provides inadequate anticoagulation for the mitral position.
  • ❌ 3.0 represents the lower end of the acceptable range for a mechanical mitral valve but would not be the optimal target. Aiming for this level could result in periods of inadequate anticoagulation.
  • ❌ 4.0 represents the upper end of the therapeutic range. While this level of anticoagulation would protect against thrombosis, maintaining an INR this high increases the risk of bleeding complications unnecessarily. The optimal balance between preventing thrombosis and avoiding bleeding is achieved with a target of 3.5.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Pulmonary hypertension is now mean PAP >20 mmHg at rest.

Calling it arterial additionally requires

PVR >2 Wood units and a wedge pressure ≤15 mmHg.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D018 — Cardiology · Pulmonary embolism
questions.questionStem: What is this new medication's mechanism of action?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 35-year-old woman is visiting the pulmonary hypertension (PAH) clinic. She is experiencing worsening shortness of breath even after starting medications. As a result, she was prescribed a combination of tadalafil and bosentan as standard therapy. However, due to her liver function being deranged, bosentan was replaced with ambrisentan. The patient was informed that the new medication is not recommended during pregnancy because of its teratogenic effects. The most common side effects of this drug are lower limb oedema, headache, and anaemia.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
Idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a rare condition that is most commonly found in young to middle-aged women. A diagnosis of idiopathic PAH is based on several investigations, including autoimmune screens, echocardiogram, cross-sectional imaging, and right heart catheterisation.

In patients with idiopathic PAH, a selective endothelin receptor A antagonist, such as ambrisentan, is typically started along with a phosphodiesterase 5 inhibitor (PDE5-i) such as tadalafil when vasoreactivity testing is negative. It should be noted that bosentan has a higher incidence of causing deranged liver function compared to ambrisentan. A common side effect of these medications is peripheral oedema. Additionally, endothelial receptor antagonists have teratogenic effects, and should not be used during pregnancy.

For patients with PAH who have tested positive for vasoreactivity during a right heart catheterisation, a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, such as amlodipine, is used. A positive vasoreactivity test is defined as a reduction in mean pulmonary artery pressure by ≥ 10- mmHg to reach an absolute value ≤ 40-mmHg, with increased or unchanged cardiac output. Calcium channel blockers alone typically suffice for positive vasoreactivity testers. If amlodipine is to be stopped, a gradual dose reduction is advised due to the possible haemodynamic worsening due to a withdrawal effect.

A PDE5-i such as tadalafil is used in patients with PAH either alone or in combination with endothelial receptor antagonists for initial treatment when they are non-responders to vasoreactivity testing. However, PDE5-i medications should not be used in combination with either nitrates or soluble guanylate cyclase stimulators due to the risk of systemic hypotension. Side effects include headache, hypotension, and flushing.

In patients with PAH who experience clinical deterioration or have an initial presentation suggesting severe pulmonary hypertension, a prostacyclin receptor agonist such as selexipag is used in combination with PDE5-i inhibitors and endothelin receptor antagonists. However, its use would depend on individual patient factors. The side effects of selexipag include headache, diarrhoea, nausea, and jaw pain. It should not be used during pregnancy.

A soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator such as riociguat is used in place of PDE5-i in certain patients with PAH, i.e., clinical deterioration despite double or triple combination therapy. These medications would not be used as initial standard therapy. Riociguat cannot be used in combination with PDE5-i due to the risk of systemic hypotension. Side effects of riociguat include hypotension, peripheral oedema, and anaemia. It is not advised for use during pregnancy.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Topic: Cardiology, Pulmonary embolism

💎 The Pearl

Apixaban or rivaroxaban are first-line for confirmed PE and DVT — no lead-in heparin needed, unlike dabigatran and edoxaban which require 5 days of LMWH first.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D019 — Cardiology · Ventricular tachycardia
questions.questionStem: How should his DVT be treated?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

Mr Brown is a 62-year-old man with colon cancer. He is undergoing adjuvant chemotherapy, however in the past six months has suffered four deep vein thrombotic (DVT) events, despite being optimally anti- coagulated with the maximum dose of dabigatran. On one occasion he suffered a DVT during treatment with dalteparin (a low molecular weight heparin) . He has been admitted with symptoms of another DVT.

#MRCP #Question

options.text: Initiate end of life drugs and prepare the family
Increase the dose of dabigatran off-licence
Insert an inferior vena caval filter

questions.correctAnswerText: Insert an inferior vena caval filter
questions.explanationHtml:
Why this is correct


This patient has recurrent DVT despite adequate anticoagulation, including maximum-dose dabigatran and a previous episode while on LMWH. In recurrent proximal DVT or PE despite adequate anticoagulation, an inferior vena cava filter may be considered after reviewing alternative anticoagulation strategies.


💡 Key exam point


Consider an inferior vena cava filter for recurrent proximal DVT or PE despite adequate anticoagulation, only after considering alternatives such as high-intensity warfarin or switching to LMWH.


Option review


- A. Add apixaban — Not best. He has already had recurrent thrombosis despite therapeutic anticoagulation, including LMWH.


- B. Initiate end-of-life drugs and prepare the family — Not indicated. The stem does not suggest that an end-of-life pathway is appropriate.


- C. Increase the dose of dabigatran off-licence — Not appropriate. He is already on the maximum dose, and increasing beyond recommended levels may cause harm.


- D. Prescribe TED stockings — Not appropriate for treating recurrent DVT. They may be used for prophylaxis in selected settings but do not treat established recurrent thrombosis.


- E. Insert an inferior vena caval filter — Correct. This is the most appropriate option given recurrent VTE despite adequate anticoagulation.


#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Topic: Cardiology, Ventricular tachycardia

💎 The Pearl

Broad-complex tachycardia — features that mean ventricular, not aberrancy:

  • AV dissociation (independent P waves; cannon a waves)
  • Capture and fusion beats
  • Positive or negative concordance across the chest leads
  • QRS >160 ms, extreme axis

Structural heart disease or previous MI makes VT overwhelmingly likely — treat broad-complex tachycardia as VT until proven otherwise.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D020 — Cardiology · ACE inhibitors
questions.questionStem: What is the likely arrhythmia?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 70-year-old man is brought to the emergency department. He is unable to provide a clear history, but a recent prescription in his wallet shows that he is taking aspirin, ramipril, furosemide and spironolactone.

🩺 Examination:

He is unwell with a cool periphery and blood pressure of 70/40 mmHg.

🔬 Investigations:

The electrocardiogram (ECG) shows a regular broad-complex tachycardia with a rate of 190 bpm. Arterial blood gas analyses are done in the emergency department and show increased levels of urea, potassium, as well as acidosis.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
Why this is correct


In an older patient with structural heart disease, a broad‑complex tachycardia should be treated as VT until proven otherwise—especially when haemodynamically compromised.


💡 Key exam point


Broad‑complex tachycardia + cardiac history = VT until proven otherwise.


Option review


- A. Atrial fibrillation (AF) — Usually irregularly irregular and typically not sustained >150 bpm through the AV node.


- B. Atrial flutter with 2:1 block — Often ~150 bpm with sawtooth flutter waves.


- C. SVT with aberrant conduction — Possible, but in this context assume VT; look for AV dissociation/capture/fusion beats.


- D. Ventricular tachycardia (VT) — Most likely with structural heart disease.


- E. Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome — Baseline short PR + delta wave; not the best fit here.


#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡


Topic: Cardiology, ACE inhibitors



💎 The Pearl


Core rule — ACE inhibitor cough (and angioedema) is bradykinin‑mediated.


Do — Stop the ACE inhibitor; switch to an ARB if RAAS blockade is still needed.


Avoid / trap — Don’t mis-treat it as allergy/asthma; it’s not histamine‑mediated.


Memory hook — “ACE breaks down bradykinin; block ACE → bradykinin builds up.”


#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D021 — Cardiology · Adrenaline
questions.questionStem: Accumulation of which one of the following proteins is responsible for this?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 51-year-old man is started on lisinopril after being found to have an average blood pressure of 154/93 on ambulatory blood pressure monitoring. Around two weeks after starting treatment he represents with a persistent dry cough.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
Why this is correct


ACE inhibitors like lisinopril block the breakdown of bradykinin as well as angiotensin I. The resulting bradykinin accumulation in the airways is responsible for the persistent dry cough seen in up to 20% of patients.


💡 Key exam point


ACE inhibitor cough is a bradykinin-mediated class effect — switch to an ARB (e.g. losartan), which spares bradykinin metabolism.


Option review


- A. Adenosine — Incorrect — causes transient AV block/flushing when given for SVT; not implicated in ACE inhibitor cough.


- B. Histamine — Incorrect — mediates allergic/anaphylactic reactions, not this mechanism.


- C. Bradykinin — Correct — accumulates due to reduced ACE-mediated degradation, triggering the cough.


- D. Acetylcholine — Incorrect — causes bronchoconstriction via M3 receptors; not the ACE inhibitor cough mechanism.


- E. Neurokinin A — Incorrect — a tachykinin involved in neurogenic inflammation, not the primary mediator here.


#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡


Topic: Cardiology, Adrenaline



💎 The Pearl


Adrenaline timing in cardiac arrest depends on the rhythm:


- Non-shockable — give 1 mg (10 mL of 1:10,000) IV as soon as possible.


- Shockable — hold until after the 3rd shock.


- Repeat every 3–5 minutes in both cases.


#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D022 — Cardiology · Adenosine diphosphate (ADP) receptor inhibitors
questions.questionStem: What is the most appropriate dose of adrenaline to give during a cardiac arrest?
questions.explanationHtml:
Why this is correct


10ml of the 1:10,000 preparation contains 1mg of adrenaline. From the BNF: Adrenaline (epinephrine) 1 in 10 000 (100 micrograms/mL) is recommended in a dose of 1 mg (10 mL) by intravenous injection repeated every 3-5 minutes if necessary.


💡 Key exam point


The cardiac arrest dose is 1mg IV = 10ml of 1:10,000, repeated every 3-5 minutes if necessary.


Option review


- A. 1ml 1:100,000 IV — delivers only 10 micrograms; far below the 1mg arrest dose.


- B. 10ml 1:1,000 IV — delivers 10mg; ten times the recommended arrest dose.


- C. 0.5ml 1:1,000 IM — 500 micrograms by the intramuscular route, not the intravenous arrest dose.


- D. 1ml 1:10,000 IV — delivers only 100 micrograms; one tenth of the required dose.


- E. 10ml 1:10,000 IV — delivers 1mg, the recommended intravenous cardiac arrest dose.


#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡


Topic: Cardiology, Adenosine diphosphate (ADP) receptor inhibitors



💎 The Pearl


Three P2Y12 inhibitors, three distinguishing features:


- Clopidogrel — a prodrug needing CYP2C19 activation; loss-of-function variants blunt its effect.


- Ticagrelor — reversible binding, not a prodrug; causes dyspnoea and bradycardia.


- Prasugrel — contraindicated after stroke/TIA; caution from age 75 due to bleeding risk.


#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D023 — Cardiology · Adult advanced life support
questions.questionStem: How does this agent inhibit platelet activation to prevent the recurrence of plaque build-up?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 55-year-old man attends with chest pain. He is given aspirin and unfractionated heparin. He undergoes emergency PCI with a drug- eluting stent. You decide to start the patient on ticagrelor.

🔬 Investigations:

An ECG and troponin confirm the diagnosis of an ST-elevation myocardial infarction.

#MRCP #Question

options.text: Bind directly to thrombin and block its interaction with its substrates
Inhibition of the platelet transmembrane receptor glycoprotein IIb/IIIa
Irreversibly binding with the platelet P2Y12 ADP receptor to prevent signal transduction
Permanently and selectively inactivating platelet cyclooxygenase 1 (COX-1), thus blocking thromboxane synthesis
Reversibly binding with the platelet P2Y12 ADP receptor to prevent signal transduction

questions.correctAnswerText: Reversibly binding with the platelet P2Y12 ADP receptor to prevent signal transduction
questions.explanationHtml:
Why this is correct

Ticagrelor reversibly binds the platelet P2Y12 ADP receptor, blocking ADP-mediated signal transduction and preventing platelet activation and aggregation — the intended antiplatelet effect after primary PCI for STEMI.

💡 Key exam point

Unlike the thienopyridines (clopidogrel, prasugrel), which bind P2Y12 irreversibly, ticagrelor's binding is reversible — relevant when timing surgery or switching antiplatelet agents.

Option review

- A. Bind directly to thrombin and block its interaction with its substrates — Incorrect; describes direct thrombin inhibitors (dabigatran, bivalirudin, argatroban), which are anticoagulants, not antiplatelets.

- B. Inhibition of the platelet transmembrane receptor glycoprotein IIb/IIIa — Incorrect; describes GPIIb/IIIa inhibitors (abciximab, eptifibatide, tirofiban), which block fibrinogen binding to the receptor.

- C. Irreversibly binding with the platelet P2Y12 ADP receptor to prevent signal transduction — Incorrect; describes the thienopyridines (clopidogrel, prasugrel), whose P2Y12 inhibition is irreversible.

- D. Permanently and selectively inactivating platelet cyclooxygenase 1 (COX-1), thus blocking thromboxane synthesis — Incorrect; describes aspirin's mechanism of action.

- E. Reversibly binding with the platelet P2Y12 ADP receptor to prevent signal transduction — Correct; this is ticagrelor's mechanism of action.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Topic: Cardiology, Adult advanced life support

💎 The Pearl

- In refractory VF/pulseless VT, give amiodarone 300 mg after the third shock, with a further 150 mg after the fifth shock.

- Lidocaine 100 mg is the alternative if amiodarone is unavailable.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D024 — Cardiology · Amiodarone
questions.questionStem: What is the most appropriate immediate management following the third shock?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 58-year-old man collapses in the emergency department. CPR is commenced immediately. The initial rhythm shows ventricular fibrillation. Two shocks have been delivered with 2 minutes of CPR between each shock. The rhythm check after the second period of CPR still shows ventricular fibrillation.

#MRCP #Question

options.text: Adrenaline 1mg IV followed immediately by amiodarone 300mg IV

questions.correctAnswerText: Adrenaline 1mg IV followed immediately by amiodarone 300mg IV
questions.explanationHtml:
Why this is correct

Adrenaline 1mg IV gives immediate inotropic and vasoconstrictive support to maintain coronary and cerebral perfusion during ongoing CPR, while amiodarone 300mg IV given immediately after provides antiarrhythmic action to help terminate VF. Current Resuscitation Council guidelines call for both drugs together in the CPR cycle following the third unsuccessful shock.

💡 Key exam point

After the 3rd shock in refractory VF/pulseless VT: give adrenaline 1mg IV + amiodarone 300mg IV together, then repeat adrenaline every 3–5 min and give a further amiodarone 150mg after the 5th shock.

Option review

- A. Adrenaline 1mg IV — right drug, wrong step; incomplete without amiodarone given immediately after.

- B. Amiodarone 300mg IV — right drug, wrong step; incomplete without adrenaline, which maintains perfusion during CPR.

- C. Adrenaline 1mg IV followed immediately by amiodarone 300mg IV — correct; the guideline-directed combination after the third shock in refractory VF.

- D. Magnesium sulphate 2g IV — not routine; reserved for hypomagnesaemia, torsades de pointes, or digoxin toxicity.

- E. Lidocaine 1.5mg/kg IV — alternative antiarrhythmic only if amiodarone is unavailable or per local protocol.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Topic: Cardiology, Amiodarone toxicity

💎 The Pearl

Amiodarone toxicity — organ by organ:

- Thyroid: both hypo- and hyperthyroidism (it's an iodine-rich molecule)

- Lung: pneumonitis progressing to fibrosis

- Liver: transaminitis, occasionally hepatitis

- Eye: corneal microdeposits (usually benign), optic neuropathy

- Skin: photosensitivity, slate-grey discolouration

Its half-life runs to weeks, so effects and interactions persist long after stopping.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D025 — Cardiology · Aortic dissection
questions.questionStem: What is the reason for this dosing strategy?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 63-year-old woman was successfully cardioverted for an unstable broad complex tachycardia. The cardiologist decides to commence oral amiodarone at 200mg three times a day, and wean at weekly intervals until a maintenance dose of 200mg once daily.

#MRCP #Question

options.text: Amiodarone has a very long half-life
For monitoring of adverse effects as an inpatient
It is metabolised and excreted rapidly by the kidneys
To reduce the risk and severity of adverse effects

questions.correctAnswerText: Amiodarone has a very long half-life
questions.explanationHtml:
Why this is correct

Oral amiodarone has poor bioavailability, so a loading regimen is used to reach therapeutic levels quickly before stepping down to a maintenance dose. Its plasma half-life is 20–100 days, so its effects and drug interactions persist for months after it is stopped.

💡 Key exam point

Because of the long half-life, monitor thyroid function tests (TFTs) and liver function tests (LFTs) every 6 months, continuing up to 12 months after amiodarone is stopped.

Option review

- A. Amiodarone has a short half-life — Incorrect; the opposite is true, its half-life is very long.

- C. For monitoring of adverse effects as an inpatient — Incorrect; the loading regime can be managed as an outpatient, with routine TFT/LFT monitoring rather than admission.

- D. It is metabolised and excreted rapidly by the kidneys — Incorrect; amiodarone is metabolised and excreted via the liver and biliary system, so it is not removed by dialysis.

- E. To reduce the risk and severity of adverse effects — Incorrect; loading speeds attainment of therapeutic levels but does not reduce long-term adverse effect risk, and nausea/vomiting are actually more common during loading.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Topic: Cardiology, Aortic dissection

💎 The Pearl

Stanford classification drives management:

- Type A — involves the ascending aorta → surgical emergency

- Type B — confined to the descending aorta → medical management with aggressive blood pressure and heart-rate control; surgery reserved for complications

Both types need rate control before vasodilators, so reflex tachycardia does not increase aortic wall shear stress.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D026 — Cardiology · Aortic regurgitation
questions.questionStem: What is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 68-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with sudden- onset, severe chest pain radiating to his back.

🩺 Examination:

He is diaphoretic and hypertensive with a blood pressure of 210/120 mmHg.

🔬 Investigations:

His ECG shows sinus tachycardia. Chest X-ray reveals a widened mediastinum. CT angiography confirms a Stanford type A aortic dissection.

#MRCP #Question

options.text: Intravenous labetalol followed by surgical repair

questions.correctAnswerText: Intravenous labetalol followed by surgical repair
questions.explanationHtml:
Why this is correct

This is a Stanford type A aortic dissection — a surgical emergency. Severe hypertension must first be controlled (target systolic 100–120 mmHg) with IV labetalol, which provides combined alpha/beta blockade to reduce both blood pressure and dP/dt, before proceeding to definitive surgical repair.

💡 Key exam point

Stanford type A dissections (involving the ascending aorta) require surgical repair; type B (descending aorta only) are managed medically unless complicated.

Why the others are wrong

- A. Immediate surgical repair — Proceeding to theatre without first controlling severe hypertension risks extending or rupturing the dissection during induction; BP must be controlled first.

- C. Intravenous labetalol and conservative management — Conservative management is reserved for type B dissections; type A requires surgery after BP control.

- D. Intravenous thrombolysis — Absolutely contraindicated; dissolves any protective clot and risks catastrophic bleeding or rupture.

- E. Intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion — Causes venodilation with reflex tachycardia, worsening shear stress; beta-blockade is preferred first-line.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Topic: Cardiology, Aortic regurgitation

💎 The Pearl

Eponymous signs of a wide pulse pressure in aortic regurgitation:

- Corrigan's sign — visible carotid pulsation; de Musset's sign — head nodding

- Quincke's sign — nailbed capillary pulsation; Traube's sign — pistol-shot femorals

- Austin Flint murmur — mid-diastolic rumble from the regurgitant jet striking the anterior mitral valve leaflet

Asymptomatic severe AR is referred for surgery once LVEF <55% or end-systolic diameter >50 mm.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D027 — Cardiology · Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy
questions.questionStem: Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 32-year-old man is recently diagnosed with ankylosing spondylitis.

🔬 Investigations:

Echocardiogram shows a valvular abnormality.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
Why this is correct

Ankylosing spondylitis is strongly associated with aortic regurgitation (occurring in around 4% of cases). Chronic inflammation causes aortitis, leading to aortic root dilatation and failure of valve leaflet coaptation, producing regurgitation. The same mechanism occurs in other seronegative and inflammatory arthritides, including rheumatoid arthritis.

💡 Key exam point

Chronic aortic regurgitation classically presents with a collapsing pulse and wide pulse pressure, plus the eponymous signs (Corrigan's, de Musset's, Quincke's, Duroziez's); echocardiography is the key investigation, and beta-blockers should be avoided as they prolong diastole and worsen the regurgitant fraction.

Why the others are wrong

- B. Aortic stenosis — usually due to valve calcification or rheumatic fever, exacerbated by hypertension and diabetes; no specific link to ankylosing spondylitis.

- C. Mitral regurgitation — associated with rheumatic fever, Marfan syndrome, and cardiomyopathy, not ankylosing spondylitis.

- D. Mitral stenosis — almost always due to rheumatic heart disease; no specific link to ankylosing spondylitis.

- E. Tricuspid stenosis — an uncommon valvular defect, usually rheumatic in origin; no association with ankylosing spondylitis.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Topic: Cardiology, Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy

💎 The Pearl

- ARVC is caused by fibrofatty replacement of the right ventricular myocardium, due to desmosome gene mutations.

- Look for an epsilon wave and T-wave inversion in V1–V3 on ECG.

- The autosomal recessive form, with woolly hair and palmoplantar keratoderma, is Naxos disease.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D028 — Cardiology · Aspirin
questions.questionStem: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 22-year-old male university student is reviewed after a single episode of pre-syncope while playing football. He is otherwise fit and well with no significant past medical or family history. An ECG is performed which demonstrates sinus rhythm with T wave inversion in leads V1, V2, and V3.

🩺 Examination:

His clinical examination is unremarkable.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
Why this is correct

ARVC is an inherited cardiomyopathy characterised by fibrofatty replacement of the right ventricular myocardium, predisposing to ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death, and is a significant cause of sudden death in young athletes. Exertional pre-syncope in a young, fit individual is a major red flag for an underlying inherited cardiac condition.

💡 Key exam point

T-wave inversion in the right precordial leads (V1-V3) in a person over 14 years of age is a major criterion in the 2010 Task Force Criteria for diagnosing ARVC, reflecting the underlying structural right ventricular disease.

Why the others are wrong

- B. Brugada syndrome — The characteristic ECG pattern is coved ST-segment elevation ≥2 mm in V1/V2 followed by a negative T-wave (the 'Type 1' pattern), possibly unmasked by fever or certain drugs; the stem describes isolated T-wave inversion, not this ST-elevation morphology.

- C. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy — The most common cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes, with an abnormal ECG in over 90% of cases, but T-wave inversion is typically deep and lateral (V4-V6, I, aVL) reflecting LV hypertrophy, whereas isolated V1-V3 inversion is more specific for right ventricular pathology.

- D. Pulmonary embolism — Can cause right heart strain with sinus tachycardia, new right bundle branch block, the S1Q3T3 pattern, and right precordial T-wave inversion, but a PE severe enough to cause pre-syncope would usually leave persistent symptoms (dyspnoea, tachycardia, pleuritic chest pain), none of which are described.

- E. Benign early repolarisation — Typically shows J-point elevation and ST-segment elevation in the precordial leads; V1-V3 T-wave inversion can be a normal juvenile variant but is a diagnosis of exclusion, and would be inappropriate to assume given the red-flag symptom of exertional pre-syncope.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Topic: Cardiology, Aspirin

💎 The Pearl

Aspirin acetylates COX-1 irreversibly, so platelet thromboxane A₂ production cannot recover — the effect lasts the platelet's 7–10 day lifespan. The ACS loading dose is 300 mg.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D029 — Cardiology · Atrial septal defect
questions.questionStem: What is the mechanism of action of aspirin to achieve an antiplatelet effect?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A patient is given aspirin 300 mg after developing an acute coronary syndrome.

#MRCP #Question

options.text: Inhibits the production of thromboxane A2
Inhibits ADP binding to its platelet receptor
Inhibits the production of prostaglandin H2

questions.correctAnswerText: Inhibits the production of thromboxane A2
questions.explanationHtml:
Why this is correct

Aspirin irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1) in platelets, blocking the conversion of arachidonic acid to thromboxane A2 — a potent vasoconstrictor and platelet aggregator. Loss of thromboxane A2 production is aspirin's key antiplatelet mechanism.

💡 Key exam point

Aspirin's antiplatelet effect is irreversible and lasts the lifespan of the platelet (~7–10 days), since platelets cannot resynthesize COX-1.

Why the others are wrong

- B. Inhibits ADP binding to its platelet receptor — this is the mechanism of P2Y12 inhibitors (clopidogrel, prasugrel, ticagrelor), not aspirin.

- C. Inhibits the production of prostaglandin H2 — COX-1 inhibition does block PGH2 formation, but PGH2 itself is not the mediator responsible for platelet aggregation; thromboxane A2 downstream of it is.

- D. Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor antagonist — this describes drugs like abciximab and eptifibatide, which block fibrinogen cross-linking of platelets, not aspirin's mechanism.

- E. Inhibits the production of prostacyclin (PGI2) — PGI2 is a vasodilator and platelet inhibitor; suppressing it would be harmful, and aspirin's antiplatelet benefit comes from thromboxane A2 suppression, not PGI2 suppression.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Topic: Cardiology, Atrial septal defect

💎 The Pearl

Two defects, two ECGs:

- Ostium secundum (commonest) — right axis deviation, incomplete RBBB

- Ostium primum — left axis deviation, prolonged PR; part of the atrioventricular septal defect spectrum, so mitral or tricuspid valve abnormality is common

Both give fixed splitting of S2 and an ejection systolic murmur from increased flow across a normal pulmonary valve.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D030 — Cardiology · Heart failure
questions.questionStem: What is the most likely underlying cardiac abnormality?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 36-year-old woman presents with a cerebral infarct following treatment for a deep vein thrombosis.

🩺 Examination:

Cardiovascular examination is entirely normal

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
Why this is correct

The clinical scenario describes a paradoxical embolus – one that has travelled from the venous system into the arterial circulation. For this to occur, there must be a shunt of some kind. PFOs are very common – estimates suggest 1 in 4 people have a PFO – making this far more likely than the other conditions listed. The shunt is not open the majority of the time; it is merely a potential space. When right atrial pressure exceeds left atrial pressure it opens and allows venous debris to enter the arterial circulation, typically during valsalva – such as straining at stool, childbirth and diving. PFO has no findings on routine clinical examination, as in this patient, whereas the other potential answers often do.

💡 Key exam point

PFOs require valsalva during an echocardiographic bubble study (agitated saline) to be visualised – saline given into a vein fills the right atrium with bubbles, and valsalva causes bubbles to cross into the left atrium if a PFO is present.

Why the others are wrong

- A. Common atrium — a patient with a common atrium would not have a normal cardiovascular exam.

- B. Ostium primum atrial septal defect — patients with ASD (primum or secundum) have fixed splitting of the second heart sound, may have an ejection systolic murmur of increased pulmonary flow, and show RBBB on ECG.

- C. Ostium secundum — patients have fixed splitting of the second heart sound and may have an ejection systolic murmur of increased pulmonary flow, making this unlikely in a patient with a normal cardiovascular exam.

- D. Partial anomalous pulmonary venous drainage — one to three pulmonary veins drain into the right atrium rather than the left, with no increased risk of right-to-left shunting; these patients may be cyanosed and clubbed.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Topic: Cardiology, Heart failure

💎 The Pearl

Sacubitril inhibits neprilysin, the enzyme that degrades natriuretic peptides — so BNP rises on treatment while NT-proBNP does not, which is why NT-proBNP remains the monitoring assay.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D031 — Cardiology · Bradyarrhythmias
questions.questionStem: What is its mechanism of action in heart failure?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

The neprilysin inhibitor, sacubitril, in combination with the angiotensin II receptor blocker, valsartan, has been shown to reduce mortality, reduce hospitalisations and improve symptoms in comparison to enalapril in the treatment of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.

#MRCP #Question

options.text: Prevents the degradation of natriuretic peptides such as BNP and ANP
Multiple inhibition of renin, angiotensinogen and aldosterone
Inhibition of vasopressin release therefore promoting diuresis

questions.correctAnswerText: Prevents the degradation of natriuretic peptides such as BNP and ANP
questions.explanationHtml:
The correct answer is prevents the degradation of natriuretic peptides such as BNP and ANP.

The natriuretic peptide system regulates the detrimental effects of the upregulation of the renin-angiotensinogen-aldosterone system (RAAS) which occurs in heart failure. Sodium and water retention and vasoconstriction caused by activation of the RAAS, sympathetic nervous system and the action of vasopressin, lead to increased ventricular preload and afterload and elevated wall stress which in turn lead to production of BNP. BNP acts to promote natriuresis and vasodilation. Atrial stretch leads to the production of ANP which has similar biological properties to BNP. Two strategies have been employed to try and improve outcomes in heart failure via modulation of this pathway. The first is the administration of exogenous natriuretic peptides. Nesiritide, a recombinant human BNP, initially showed promising beneficial effects on haemodynamics and natriuresis in patients with HF. However, in a large- scale randomised controlled trial, it failed to improve outcomes though it did improve dyspnoea. The second strategy is to inhibit the breakdown of natriuretic peptides. ANP & BNP are inactivated by a membrane bound endopeptidase, neprilysin, which is found in a number of tissues but in especially high concentrations in the kidney. This led to the development of the neprilysin inhibitor, sacubitril. Given in combination with the angiotensin II receptor blocker, valsartan, it has been shown to reduce mortality, reduce hospitalisations and improve symptoms in comparison to enalapril in the treatment of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Atropine 500 micrograms IV, repeated every 3–5 minutes to a maximum of 3 mg, for bradycardia with adverse signs. Beyond that: isoprenaline, adrenaline infusion, or transcutaneous pacing.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D032 — Cardiology · Brugada syndrome
questions.questionStem: Which one of the following is the most appropriate piece of advice?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

You are called to see a man who is due for elective right hemicolectomy for a Duke B colonic carcinoma. He is totally asymptomatic.

🔬 Investigations:

His admission ECG shows atrioventricular dissociation with a ventricular response of 40 bpm.

#MRCP #Question

options.text: Do nothing and let the operation go ahead as planned tomorrow
Insert a temporary pacemaker before the operation
Perform an exercise test before the operation
Postpone the operation and refer for an outpatient permanent pacemaker
Start an infusion of isoprenaline an hour before the operation

questions.correctAnswerText: Insert a temporary pacemaker before the operation
questions.explanationHtml:
Pacing

Atrioventricular dissociation is part of a spectrum of diagnoses that includes complete heart block. Performing a large operation during complete heart block risks haemodynamic compromise. Although he is not symptomatic and is not profoundly bradycardic at present, vagal tone can increase intraoperatively, which may compromise his cardiac output. It would be appropriate to place a temporary pacing wire (ideally via the jugular approach). Therefore insertion of a temporary pacemaker before the operation is the best answer here as it enables the operation to proceed without delay and the temporary pacing wire can be changed to a pacemaker at a later date.

Temporary pacing

Indications for temporary pacing include: symptomatic bradycardia that is not improved by atropine complete heart block causing or at risk of haemodynamic compromise suppression of tachyarrhythmias that are not amenable to drug therapy (to enable overdrive pacing).

Permanent pacing

Permanent pacing is required for: complete heart block drug-resistant tachyarrhythmias Mobitz type II heart block persistent AV conduction block post MI sick sinus syndrome.

Patients with trifascicular block should be considered for permanent pacing if there is evidence of: syncope other cardiac symptoms attributable to AV block evidence of complete heart block.

  • ❌ A. Do nothing and let the operation go ahead as planned tomorrow — Do nothing and let the operation go ahead as planned tomorrow is incorrect. As described, vagal tone can increase intraoperatively which may compromise his cardiac output ruling this option out as the best answer.
  • ❌ C. Perform an exercise test before the operation — Perform an exercise test before the operation is incorrect. An exercise test would be unhelpful in this setting.
  • ❌ D. Postpone the operation and refer for an outpatient permanent pacemaker — Postpone the operation and refer for an outpatient permanent pacemaker is incorrect. A Duke B carcinoma has extended through the bowel wall, making a quick operation necessary. Delaying the operation for an outpatient referral is inappropriate.
  • ❌ E. Start an infusion of isoprenaline an hour before the operation — Start an infusion of isoprenaline an hour before the operation is incorrect. Isoprenaline can be used as an adjunct to increase heart rate in bradycardic patients but would used if temporary pacing was not available.42029

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Coved ST elevation in V1–V2 with T-wave inversion, from loss-of-function SCN5A mutations. The pattern can be unmasked by fever or by a class Ic drug such as flecainide.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D033 — Cardiology · Calcium channel blockers
questions.questionStem: Which of the following proteins is most likely to be dysfunctional?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 32-year-old man of Filipino descent is reviewed in the cardiology clinic following a syncopal episode at home during a febrile illness. He has no other medical history.

🩺 Examination:

His physical examination is unremarkable.

🔬 Investigations:

An ECG shows an incomplete right bundle branch block pattern with coved ST- segment elevation of 2.5mm in lead V1, followed by a negative T-wave.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
Myocardial sodium ion channel protein is the correct answer. The clinical presentation of syncope with a febrile trigger in a young man of Southeast Asian descent, combined with the classic ECG findings of coved ST-elevation in V1 ('Brugada type 1' pattern), is highly suggestive of Brugada syndrome. This condition is an inherited channelopathy most commonly caused by a loss-of-function mutation in the SCN5A gene, which encodes the alpha subunit of the myocardial sodium ion channel. This defect alters the cardiac action potential, particularly in the right ventricular outflow tract, causing the characteristic ECG changes and predisposing to life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias.

  • ❌ Myocardial potassium ion channel protein mutations (e.g., KCNQ1, KCNH2) are primarily associated with Long QT syndrome. While this is another inherited channelopathy that can cause syncope, the ECG is characterised by a prolonged QT interval, not the coved ST-elevation and RBBB pattern seen in this patient.
  • ❌ Ryanodine receptor dysfunction (due to RYR2 gene mutations) is the underlying cause of catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (CPVT). This condition typically presents with syncope or sudden death during exercise or emotional stress due to adrenergically- mediated ventricular arrhythmias. The resting ECG is usually normal, which is not the case here.
  • ❌ Cardiac troponin T is a sarcomeric protein involved in muscle contraction. Mutations in the TNNT2 gene are a cause of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM). While HCM can present with syncope, the ECG would typically show features of left ventricular hypertrophy, such as large voltage criteria and deep T-wave inversions, which are not described in this scenario.
  • ❌ Desmoplakin is a desmosomal protein crucial for myocyte adhesion. Mutations in genes encoding desmosomal proteins cause arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC). The ECG in ARVC may show T-wave inversion in the right precordial leads (V1-V3) and characteristic findings like an epsilon wave, but not the specific coved ST-elevation of Brugada syndrome.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

The split that matters clinically:

  • Dihydropyridines (amlodipine, nifedipine) — vascular selective; ankle oedema, flushing, reflex tachycardia
  • Rate-limiting (verapamil, diltiazem) — negatively inotropic and chronotropic; verapamil causes constipation

Verapamil with a beta-blocker risks profound bradycardia, heart block and heart failure — when combining with a beta-blocker, always choose a dihydropyridine.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D034 — Cardiology · Cardiac Arrest
questions.questionStem: Which one of the following drugs is most likely to be responsible?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 54-year-old man with hypertension is reviewed in clinic. He complains that over the past two months he has developed ankle swelling.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
Amlodipine is the archetypal dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker and peripheral ankle oedema is its hallmark adverse effect, occurring in up to 10–15 % of patients. The drug selectively relaxes precapillary arterioles, increasing hydrostatic pressure within capillaries while leaving post-capillary venous tone unchanged. This pressure gradient pushes fluid into the interstitial space, producing painless, pitting oedema that typically appears after a few weeks of therapy and is bilateral. The phenomenon is dose-related, improves on stopping the drug or switching to a different antihypertensive class, and is not due to salt and water retention, so diuretics are usually ineffective. Recognising this mechanism allows the clinician to reassure the patient and alter therapy appropriately.

  • ❌ Perindopril, an ACE inhibitor, more commonly causes cough, taste disturbance and, rarely, angio-oedema rather than dependent peripheral oedema. In fact, by reducing afterload and promoting natriuresis, ACE inhibitors can improve congestive ankle swelling secondary to heart failure. Consequently, although perindopril is a very widely used antihypertensive, it is not usually implicated when isolated ankle swelling develops in an otherwise well patient.
  • ❌ Indapamide is a thiazide-like diuretic. Its recognised adverse effects include hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, gout and a mild photosensitive rash. It promotes renal sodium and water loss, so it would be expected to relieve, not precipitate, peripheral oedema. Ankle swelling developing while on indapamide should prompt the clinician to look for another cause, such as concomitant amlodipine therapy or underlying cardiac disease.
  • ❌ Losartan, an angiotensin II receptor blocker, shares many side-effects with ACE inhibitors but ankle oedema is not a characteristic problem. By blocking the renin–angiotensin pathway it tends to reduce venous and arterial pressures and is sometimes used as part of combination therapy precisely because it does not exacerbate dihydropyridine-induced swelling.
  • ❌ Diltiazem is a non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker with more pronounced effects on the myocardium and cardiac conduction than on peripheral vasculature. Although mild ankle oedema can occur, it is far less common than with dihydropyridines like amlodipine. Bradycardia, constipation and worsening of heart failure in susceptible patients are considerably more typical. Therefore, in a patient presenting primarily with ankle swelling after starting antihypertensive therapy, diltiazem is a less likely culprit than amlodipine.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Reversible causes — four Hs, four Ts:

  • Hypoxia, Hypovolaemia, Hypo/hyperkalaemia and metabolic, Hypo/hyperthermia
  • Thrombosis (coronary or pulmonary), Tension pneumothorax, Tamponade, Toxins

When pulmonary embolism is the suspected cause, consider thrombolysis and then continue CPR for 60–90 minutes.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D035 — Cardiology · Cardiac tamponade
questions.questionStem: What is the strength (in joules) recommended for the monophasic shock used for defibrillation?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 58-year-old-woman suffers a cardiac arrest while on the ward.

🔬 Investigations:

A rhythm strip shows VF.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
The Resuscitation Council (UK) recommends that the initial energy level for the first shock with a monophasic defibrillator is 360 J.

Biphasic defibrillation is more effective that monophasic defibrillation, hence lower energies in the range of 150–200 J are recommended for the first shock. The majority of defibrillators in modern clinical practice are biphasic.

Cardiac arrest Aetiology:

Three-quarters of out of hospital cardiac arrests are due to ventricular fibrillation in patients with pre- existing heart disease, although across a general population this is only true of 20% of cardiac arrests Only a small proportion can be attributed to pulseless electrical activity (PEA); the rest are due to asystole PEA may have a potentially reversible cause:

hypovolaemia

hypoxia hyperkalaemia hypokalaemia hypothermia tension pneumothorax tamponade toxicity due to drugs thromboembolism Defibrillation:

Defibrillation is used to convert ventricular fibrillation to sinus rhythm The Resuscitation Council (UK) recommends an initial 360-J shock for a monophasic defibrillator and 150–200 J for a biphasic shock.

  • ❌ A. 50 J — 50 J is incorrect. The Resuscitation Council (UK) recommends that the initial energy level for the first shock with a monophasic defibrillator is 360 J.
  • ❌ B. 100 J — 100 J is incorrect. The Resuscitation Council (UK) recommends that the initial energy level for the first shock with a monophasic defibrillator is 360 J.
  • ❌ C. 200 J — 200 J is incorrect. The Resuscitation Council (UK) recommends that the initial energy level for the first shock with a monophasic defibrillator is 360 J.
  • ❌ D. 300 J — 300 J is incorrect. The Resuscitation Council (UK) recommends that the initial energy level for the first shock with a monophasic defibrillator is 360 J.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Tamponade versus constriction:

  • Both: raised JVP, quiet heart sounds, small-volume pulse
  • Tamponade — pulsus paradoxus, electrical alternans, absent y descent
  • Constriction — Kussmaul's sign, pericardial knock, prominent x and y descents, pericardial calcification

Beck's triad (hypotension, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds) describes tamponade.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D036 — Cardiology · Chest pain
questions.questionStem: Given the likely diagnosis, what is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 64-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 2 days of decreased exercise tolerance and progressive dyspnoea at rest. He has no significant past medical history.

🩺 Examination:

On examination, he appears short of breath. His jugular venous pressure (JVP) is visibly elevated and some peripheral oedema is noted. Heart sounds are quiet upon auscultation. His blood pressure is 96/65 mmHg, heart rate 102 bpm and respiratory rate 22 breaths/min.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
This patient has suspected cardiac tamponade. This is a medical emergency, defined by the accumulation of pericardial fluid, blood, pus or air within the pericardial space, restricting cardiac filling and output. It is classically associated with 'Beck's triad' - hypotension, raised JVP and muffled heart sounds, all of which are described here. The definitive management option for this condition is immediate pericardiocentesis; without this, it can be fatal.

  • ❌ Cardiac surgery is incorrect. This may be warranted if a type A aortic dissection was being suspected, which may present in a somewhat similar manner. However, it would present with differing blood pressures in both arms and chest pain, rather than Beck's triad.
  • ❌ Intravenous furosemide is incorrect. This would be used for pulmonary oedema. Whilst also presenting with breathlessness, crackles would instead be audible on auscultation of the chest. The most important next step is pericardiocentesis to remove the accumulated fluid from the pericardial space.
  • ❌ Oral ibuprofen is incorrect. If acute pericarditis was instead being considered, and the patient was haemodynamically stable and well, this would be an appropriate option. Pericarditis would instead have presented with chest pain that is relieved by leaning forward, rather than the numerous signs and symptoms seen here.
  • ❌ Thrombolysis is incorrect. This would be appropriate for a pulmonary embolism with right heart strain. Although there is evidence of right heart failure here - peripheral oedema - the diagnosis is more likely to be cardiac tamponade. A pulmonary embolism with right heart strain would also present with dyspnoea, but would not feature muffled heart sounds, which instead suggests tamponade.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Coronary CT angiography is the first-line investigation for new-onset stable chest pain with typical or atypical anginal features — pre-test probability scoring is no longer advised, and a zero calcium score no longer rules out coronary disease.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D037 — Cardiology · Clopidogrel
questions.questionStem: What is the most important investigation to pursue given her risk for coronary artery disease?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 79-year-old female presents to the low-risk chest pain clinic with intermittent substernal chest pains. The pain typically comes on with exertion and improves with rest. A trial of GTN has been given by her GP which helps with her pain. She is a known ex-smoker of 30 pack-years. She has no diabetes, hyperlipidaemia, hypertension, and no family history of coronary artery disease.

🩺 Examination:

On examination her observations are stable. On auscultations of her chest, her first and second heart sounds are audible with no added sounds and her lungs are clear.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
The correct answer is Contrast-enhanced coronary CT angiography. This is the most appropriate first-line investigation for this patient presenting with stable angina symptoms and low-intermediate pre-test probability for coronary artery disease (CAD) according to NICE guidelines. CT coronary angiography (CTCA) offers excellent negative predictive value and can effectively rule out significant coronary artery disease. It is non-invasive and provides detailed anatomical information about coronary arteries.

The key factors supporting CTCA as the correct choice include: - Typical angina symptoms - Low-intermediate pre-test probability based on risk factors - Current NICE guidelines recommending CTCA as first-line investigation - Non-invasive nature of the test - Excellent negative predictive value - Ability to visualize coronary anatomy directly

  • ❌ Invasive coronary angiogram would be too aggressive as a first-line investigation for stable symptoms in a patient with low-intermediate risk. This invasive procedure carries risks and is typically reserved for high-risk patients or when less invasive tests suggest significant disease requiring intervention.
  • ❌ Stress test ECG (exercise tolerance test) is no longer recommended as a first-line investigation for diagnosing stable angina according to current NICE guidelines. It has relatively poor sensitivity and specificity compared to newer imaging modalities.
  • ❌ Myocardial perfusion scintigraphy is a functional test that may be appropriate if CTCA is contraindicated or shows equivocal results. However, it wouldn't be the first-choice investigation in this scenario given the availability of CTCA.
  • ❌ No further investigations would be inappropriate given the patient's typical angina symptoms and cardiovascular risk factors (age, smoking history). Her symptoms warrant proper investigation to establish a diagnosis and guide management.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Clopidogrel is a prodrug activated by CYP2C19 — which is why omeprazole and esomeprazole reduce its effect. Lansoprazole and pantoprazole are the safer acid-suppression choices.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D038 — Cardiology · Coarctation of the Aorta
questions.questionStem: Concurrent use of which one of the following drugs may make clopidogrel less effective?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A patient who is intolerant of aspirin is started on clopidogrel for the secondary prevention of ischaemic heart disease.

#MRCP #Question

options.text: Long-term tetracycline use (e.g. For acne rosacea)

questions.explanationHtml:
The correct answer is Omeprazole. Clopidogrel is a prodrug which requires conversion into its active form by the liver enzyme CYP2C19. Omeprazole, a proton pump inhibitor (PPI), inhibits this enzyme and therefore can reduce the effectiveness of clopidogrel. This interaction has been associated with an increased risk of adverse cardiovascular events. UK guidelines recommend that patients requiring both clopidogrel and a PPI should be prescribed pantoprazole or lansoprazole instead, as these do not interact.

Warfarin does not make clopidogrel less effective. However, using them together increases the risk of bleeding because both drugs have anticoagulant effects - warfarin acts by inhibiting vitamin K-dependent clotting factors while clopidogrel prevents platelet aggregation. Therefore, their concurrent use should be carefully considered.

Codeine also does not interfere with the effectiveness of clopidogrel. But it's worth noting that both drugs can increase the risk of gastrointestinal side effects such as constipation and stomach discomfort.

Long-term use of tetracycline, for conditions like acne rosacea, doesn't impact on the efficacy of clopidogrel either. Tetracycline is an antibiotic that works by inhibiting protein synthesis in bacteria, and it doesn't interact with clopidogrel.

Finally, Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) don't make clopidogrel less effective but there is a potential interaction between these two drugs that could increase the risk of bleeding due to their individual effects on platelets - SSRIs inhibit platelet uptake of serotonin (which is needed for platelet aggregation) and clopidogrel prevents platelet aggregation by blocking ADP receptors on platelets. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear but it's generally advisable to monitor patients closely if these drugs are used together.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Coarctation of the aorta:

  • Radiofemoral delay, upper-limb hypertension, weak femoral pulses
  • Rib notching on chest X-ray from dilated intercostal collaterals
  • Strongly associated with Turner syndrome and with a bicuspid aortic valve

Untreated, it presents as resistant hypertension in a young adult.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D039 — Cardiology · Complete heart block
questions.questionStem: Which one of the following cardiac diagnoses fits best with her clinical condition?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

You are asked to review a 19-year-old woman who presents with increasing shortness of breath on exercise. She is from a family that have rarely encountered medical care. She reports that her legs feel tired all the time and she has occasional chest pain on exercising.

🩺 Examination:

On examination she appears of short stature with extra skin folds around her neck, and appears to have failure of secondary sexual development. Her blood pressure is raised at 165/100 mmHg.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
To answer this question you should recognise that the patient has Turner syndrome (indicated by the webbing of the neck and lack of secondary sexual development) and that this is strongly associated with coarctation of the aorta (indicated by pains in legs, hypertension and episodes of chest pain). In young patients with hypertension, always consider secondary causes such as coarctation. The other options do not present in this manner and therefore do not best fit the description. Turner patients often have bicuspid aortic valves – these occur as part of the abnormal aorta when there is coarctation.

Coarctation

• Coarctation is a stenosis of variable severity in the aorta – in extreme cases there can be a discontinuity in the aorta. • Bicuspid aortic valves are present in 50% of patients with coarctation.

• Turner syndrome is strongly associated with coarctation.

• Infantile type – presents early: stenosis is proximal to the left subclavian artery; hypertension is present only in the right arm.

• Adult type – presents in teens to early adulthood: stenosis is distal to the left subclavian; both arms are hypertensive; the upper body is better developed than the lower. Leg pulses are diminished or even absent. • Symptoms include: vigorous pulsation in the neck or throat hypertension tired legs or intermittent claudication on running left ventricular failure angina pectoris aortic rupture.

• Physical signs to note include: radiofemoral pulse delay development of collateral vessels – may be heard as systolic murmur over praecordium left ventricular failure ejection systolic murmur.

Electrocardiogram (ECG) shows left ventricular hypertrophy, and right bundle-branch block is common.

  • ❌ A. Aortic regurgitation — Aortic regurgitation is incorrect. As described aortic regurgitation does not present in this manner and so is not the best choice here.
  • ❌ C. Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy — Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy is incorrect. As described hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy does not present in this manner and so is not the best choice here.
  • ❌ D. Mitral regurgitation — Mitral regurgitation is incorrect. As described mitral regurgitation does not present in this manner and so is not the best choice here.
  • ❌ E. Pulmonary stenosis — Pulmonary stenosis is incorrect. As described pulmonary stenosis does not present in this manner and so is not the best choice here.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Cannon a waves and a variable-intensity first heart sound are the bedside signature of complete heart block — atria contracting at random against closed tricuspid valves.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D040 — Cardiology · Coronary Artery Bypass Grafts
questions.questionStem: Which one of the following clinical findings may also be found?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 72-year-old male is admitted to the Emergency Room following a collapse at church.

🔬 Investigations:

ECG reveals dissociation between the P and QRS complexes with a rate of 40 / minute.

#MRCP #Question

options.text: Giant v waveforms in the JVP

questions.explanationHtml:
The correct answer is variable intensity of S1. In complete heart block (third-degree AV block), there is complete dissociation between atrial and ventricular activity. This means the P waves and QRS complexes occur independently of each other. When atrial contraction (P wave) occurs very close to ventricular contraction (QRS complex), the S1 heart sound will be louder due to higher ventricular end-diastolic volume. Conversely, when atrial contraction occurs far from ventricular contraction, S1 will be softer. This creates characteristic variation in S1 intensity.

The bradycardia of 40/min and dissociated P waves and QRS complexes are classic ECG findings of complete heart block, which requires urgent temporary pacing followed by permanent pacemaker insertion in most cases.

  • ❌ Loud S1 is typically associated with conditions like mitral stenosis or short PR interval, not complete heart block. A consistently loud S1 would not be expected.
  • ❌ Narrow pulse pressure is not a typical finding in complete heart block. The slow heart rate actually tends to cause an increased pulse pressure due to increased stroke volume.
  • ❌ Giant v waveforms in the JVP are typically seen in tricuspid regurgitation, not complete heart block. The JVP may show cannon a waves due to atrial contraction against closed AV valves.
  • ❌ Soft S2 is not a characteristic finding of complete heart block. S2 intensity is more related to semilunar valve closure and arterial pressure than to AV conduction.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

The left internal mammary artery to the LAD has the best long-term patency of any graft — arterial conduits substantially outlast saphenous vein grafts.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D041 — Cardiology · DVLA
questions.questionStem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 55-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department with central crushing chest pain radiating to the left arm. He suffered a non-ST segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) three weeks earlier and was found to have a critical left anterior descending lesion, for which he underwent coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) with a saphenous vein bypass graft to his left anterior descending artery (LAD) artery. Today, he complains of symptoms similar to his previous admission with the NSTEMI. Investigations are carried out, which reveal: Widespread anterior Electrocardiogram (ECG) ST elevation

🩺 Examination:

His blood pressure today is 105/82 mmHg; pulse is 110 bpm and regular. There are crackles to the mid-zones bilaterally on auscultation. Heart sounds are normal.

🔬 Investigations:

Investigation Result Normal value

Haemoglobin (Hb) 139 g/l 135–175 g/l

White cell count (WCC) 10.0 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l

Platelets (PLT) 292 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l

Sodium (Na +) 143 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l

Potassium (K +) 5.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l

Creatinine (Cr) 122 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l

#MRCP #Question

options.text: Arterial occlusion distal to the graft insertion

questions.explanationHtml:
Early occlusion (within the first 30 days after surgery) occurs in approximately 5–10% of saphenous vein grafts performed in bypass grafting. These occlusions are usually thrombotic and are usually related to technical problems with the anastomosis, and injury to the vein related to manipulation during harvesting may also be important. Aspirin is thought to reduce the risk of early graft occlusion. Between 3% and 6% of patients suffer clinically significant ischaemia.

  • ❌ A. Arterial occlusion distal to the graft insertion — The widespread ST elevation seen here is most consistent with a proximal lesion, rather than a lesion distal to the graft insertion. A distal lesion would be more likely to create either limited lateral or septal changes on the ECG which are not reported here.
  • ❌ B. Bacterial endocarditis — Bacterial endocarditis is manifest by features of vasculitis including night sweats, weight loss, splinter haemorrhages on examination of the fingernails, and usually by a heart murmur, which is not reported here.
  • ❌ C. Post-surgery inflammatory pericarditis — Post-surgery inflammatory pericarditis is characterised by pleuritic chest pain which is relieved on sitting forward. There may be a pericardial rub on auscultation and evidence of a pericardial effusion. It is usually managed with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents (NSAIDs) or colchicine.
  • ❌ D. Pulmonary embolism — The ECG changes seen here are consistent with an acute anterior myocardial infarction. They do not fit with a large pulmonary embolism where more characteristically an S1 Q3 T3 pattern of changes would be expected. The pain reported here is also more consistent with myocardial ischaemia.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

After an acute coronary syndrome, Group 1 (car and motorcycle) licence:

  • 1 week if PCI was successful, no urgent revascularisation is planned, and LVEF is at least 40%
  • 4 weeks if any of those are not met
  • DVLA need not be notified

Group 2 (bus and lorry) is different: DVLA must be notified and relicensing takes at least 6 weeks.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D042 — Cardiology · Digoxin and digoxin toxicity
questions.questionStem: What advice should he be given regarding driving?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 54-year-old man is admitted following a myocardial infarction associated with ST elevation. He is treated with thrombolysis and does not undergo angioplasty.

#MRCP #Question

options.text: Can continue driving but must inform DVLA
Cannot drive until an angiogram has been performed and reviewed by a cardiologist

questions.explanationHtml:
The correct answer is Cannot drive for 4 weeks. According to the UK Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA) guidelines, a patient who has suffered an ST elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) and received thrombolysis but not undergone angioplasty should refrain from driving for a minimum of 4 weeks. This period allows for initial recovery and stabilisation of the patient's condition.

The first option, Can continue driving but must inform DVLA, is incorrect as it does not account for the mandatory off-road period required after STEMI. Even if the patient feels well, they are legally obliged to stop driving for at least 4 weeks following their myocardial infarction.

The second option, Cannot drive until an angiogram has been performed and reviewed by a cardiologist, is also incorrect. While an angiogram may be beneficial in assessing coronary artery disease severity, it does not determine when a person can resume driving post- STEMI according to DVLA guidelines.

The third choice, Cannot drive for 1 week, is incorrect because it significantly underestimates the recommended off-road period post- STEMI. One week is not sufficient time for most patients to recover from such a significant cardiac event.

Finally, the last option Cannot drive for 12 weeks overstates the necessary off-road period after STEMI without angioplasty. Although some conditions or complications may require longer periods before resuming driving, in general situations, four weeks is adequate according to DVLA guidelines.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Digoxin inhibits the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, raising intracellular calcium.

  • Hypokalaemia potentiates toxicity — potassium and digoxin compete for the same binding site
  • Yellow-green visual haloes, confusion, nausea, arrhythmia
  • Reverse-tick ST depression is an effect of the drug, not of toxicity

Hypomagnesaemia, hypercalcaemia and renal impairment all increase risk.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D043 — Cardiology · Dipyridamole
questions.questionStem: What is the likely mechanism of drug toxicity in this case?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 65-year-old man presents to the emergency department with shortness of breath. He has a history of heart failure and atrial fibrillation. He is on furosemide, bisoprolol, ramipril, and digoxin. He is treated with intravenous furosemide. He reports feeling unwell. He begins to vomit and reports yellow-green discoloration of his vision.

🩺 Examination:

On examination, he has bilateral crackles to the midzones.

🔬 Investigations:

Na+ 128 mmol/L (135 - 145)

K+ 2.7 mmol/L (3.5 - 5.0)

Urea 10.1 mmol/L (2.0 - 7.0)

Creatinine 111 µmol/L (55 - 120)

Calcium 2.05 mmol/L (2.20-2.60)

Troponin 3 ng//L (0-14)

TSH 2.1 mIU/L (0.4-4.0)

#MRCP #Question

options.text: Reduce volume and distribution of clearance

questions.explanationHtml:
Increased binding to ATPase pump is correct. The patient presents with nausea, vomiting, and yellow-green discoloration of vision. This suggests digoxin toxicity, which has likely been precipitated by hypokalemia secondary to furosemide treatment. Digoxin normally binds to the ATPase pump on the same site as potassium. Hypokalaemia results in digoxin more easily binding to the ATPase pump and increased inhibitory effects, Decreased binding to ATPase pump is incorrect. If digoxin is inhibited from binding to the ATPase pump, there will be fewer inhibitory effects and less toxicity risk.

Increased calcium influx is incorrect. This can cause digoxin toxicity given that calcium and digoxin have additive inotropic effects. However, in this case, the calcium is low rather than high, so this is unlikely.

Reduce volume and distribution of clearance is incorrect. This is the mechanism by which hypothyroidism predisposes to digoxin toxicity. However, this patient's TSH level is normal, so this is incorrect.

Reduced calcium influx is incorrect. It is hypercalcaemia rather than hypocalcaemia that predisposes to digoxin toxicity. This patient is hypocalcaemic so this is not the likely cause of toxicity.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Dipyridamole blocks cellular reuptake of adenosine and inhibits phosphodiesterase — so it markedly potentiates adenosine, and must be stopped before adenosine or dipyridamole stress testing is interpreted.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D044 — Cardiology · Ebstein's anomaly
questions.questionStem: What is the mechanism of action of dipyridamole?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 72-year-old man is prescribed a dipyridamole in addition to aspirin following an ischaemic stroke.

#MRCP #Question

options.text: Inhibits ADP binding to its platelet receptor

questions.explanationHtml:
The correct answer is that dipyridamole acts as a phosphodiesterase inhibitor. Phosphodiesterase inhibitor is the primary mechanism through which dipyridamole exerts its antiplatelet effect. By inhibiting phosphodiesterase, dipyridamole prevents the breakdown of cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) within platelets. Elevated levels of cAMP reduce platelet activation and aggregation. Additionally, dipyridamole blocks the cellular reuptake of adenosine, leading to increased extracellular adenosine levels, which further inhibits platelet function.

  • ❌ Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor describes the mechanism of drugs like abciximab and tirofiban, which block the final common pathway of platelet aggregation by preventing fibrinogen binding to activated platelets. This is not how dipyridamole works.
  • ❌ Inhibits ADP binding to its platelet receptor is the mechanism of action for drugs like clopidogrel and ticagrelor, which are P2Y12 receptor antagonists. These medications prevent ADP-mediated platelet activation, but this is not the mechanism of dipyridamole.
  • ❌ Agonist of thromboxane synthase is incorrect as this would promote platelet aggregation. Thromboxane A2 is a potent platelet activator, and its synthesis is actually targeted for inhibition in antiplatelet therapy, not activation.
  • ❌ Irreversibly acetylating cyclooxygenase describes the mechanism of action of aspirin, which prevents the formation of thromboxane A2 by permanently inhibiting COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes. While dipyridamole is often combined with aspirin for enhanced antiplatelet effect, this is not its mechanism of action.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Ebstein's anomaly: apical displacement of the tricuspid valve leaflets creating an 'atrialised' right ventricle. Linked to lithium exposure in pregnancy and to Wolff-Parkinson-White.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D045 — Cardiology · Eclampsia
questions.questionStem: What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 20-year-old man presents with episodes of palpitations and dyspnoea which occur at rest and last from seconds to minutes at a time. He is normally fit and well and has no significant past medical history. He drinks 8 units of alcohol per week and denies using any illegal drugs. An electrocardiogram revealed normal sinus rhythm with a delta wave pattern suggesting Wolf-Parkinson-White syndrome.

🩺 Examination:

On examination, there is a pansystolic murmur which is worse on inspiration. His heart rate is 69/min with good peripheral pulses. His chest is clear, the jugular venous pressure is not elevated and there is no peripheral oedema. Oxygen saturations are normal and there are no signs of cyanosis.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
Pre-excitation on ECG with a tricuspid regurgitation murmur are suspicious for Ebstein's abnormality, which is associated with Wolff- Parkinson-White syndrome. Ebstein's abnormality may be caused by exposure to lithium in utero. In Ebstein's abnormality the tricuspid valve leaflets are attached lower down in the right ventricle than normal. The part of the ventricle superior to the valves behaves like the right atrium ('atrialisation'). The valvules regurgitate during systole, causing enlargement of the right atrium. Increased right atrial pressure can prevent normal closure of the patent foramen ovale after birth. The time of presentation depends on the anatomy of the anomaly. It can present in neonates with cyanosis or with heart failure or an incidental murmur in childhood. It typically presents with arrhythmia in adults. Some cases of Ebstein's abnormality are associated with lithium and benzodiazepine use in pregnancy.

Ventricular septal defect (VSD) is not typically associated with Wolf- Parkinson-White syndrome and the murmur of VSD is not accentuated with inspiration. Hypertrophic obstructed cardiomyopathy is an autosomal dominant disorder of muscle tissue. It is the most common cause of sudden cardiac death in the young. It causes an ejection systolic murmur which is increased with a Valsalva manoeuvre and decreased on squatting.

Mitral regurgitation causes a blowing pansystolic murmur best heard at the apex and classically radiating to the axilla. Causes include myocardial infarction, mitral valve prolapse, infective endocarditis, rheumatic fever and congenital causes. It is accentuated on expiration and not typically associated with Wolf-Parkinson-White syndrome.

Aortic stenosis can occur in young people, particularly those with a bicuspid aortic valve. It causes an ejection systolic murmur which radiates to the carotids.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Magnesium sulfate, loading dose 4 g intravenously, is the treatment for eclamptic seizures and for prophylaxis in severe pre-eclampsia — not a conventional anticonvulsant.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D046 — Cardiology · Heparin
questions.questionStem: What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

You are called to the obstetric ward to see a woman who is fitting. She is 34-weeks pregnant and currently an inpatient for the treatment of severe pre-eclampsia. The anaesthetist has secured the airway and is giving 100% oxygen.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
