The most appropriate next step in this scenario is to administer IV magnesium sulphate. Magnesium sulphate is the first-line treatment for eclamptic seizures in pregnant women, according to UK guidelines. It has been shown to be effective in preventing recurrent seizures and reducing maternal morbidity. In severe pre-eclampsia, magnesium sulphate can also be used as a prophylactic measure to prevent the development of eclampsia.

IV calcium gluconate would not be the correct choice in this situation. Calcium gluconate is typically used as an antidote for hypermagnesemia or hypocalcemia, neither of which is indicated in this case. The patient's primary issue is an eclamptic seizure, and calcium gluconate does not have any anticonvulsant properties.

IV labetalol and IV methyldopa are both antihypertensive medications that can be used to manage hypertension in pregnancy. However, they do not address the immediate concern of the patient's ongoing seizure. While controlling blood pressure is important in managing pre- eclampsia, it should not take precedence over treating the active seizure with an appropriate anticonvulsant medication like magnesium sulphate.

IV lorazepam, a benzodiazepine, might seem like a reasonable choice since it has anticonvulsant properties and is often used to treat status epilepticus. However, it is not the first-line treatment for eclamptic seizures during pregnancy due to its potential adverse effects on both mother and fetus. Magnesium sulphate remains the preferred treatment option because it specifically targets the underlying pathophysiology of eclampsia while providing neuroprotection for both mother and baby.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Unfractionated versus low molecular weight:

  • UFH — inhibits thrombin and factor Xa via antithrombin; monitored by APTT; short half-life and fully reversible with protamine, so preferred in renal failure and high bleeding risk
  • LMWH — predominantly anti-Xa; no routine monitoring; renally cleared

Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia appears 5–10 days in, is prothrombotic despite the low platelet count, and is far commoner with UFH.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D047 — Cardiology · Flecainide
questions.questionStem: What is the most appropriate immediate management step?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 68-year-old man was admitted 7 days ago for an NSTEMI and started on therapeutic enoxaparin. He now develops a swollen, painful right calf. An urgent ultrasound confirms a deep vein thrombosis. His platelet count on admission was 220 x 109/L. His current blood results are shown. Platelets 75 x 109/L (150 - 400)

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
Commence argatroban infusion This patient has developed a new thrombosis (DVT) and a significant (>50%) drop in his platelet count, occurring 7 days after starting a heparin product (enoxaparin). This clinical picture is highly suggestive of Type II Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT), a prothrombotic, immune-mediated condition. The immediate management is to stop all forms of heparin immediately and initiate an alternative, non-heparin anticoagulant. Argatroban is a direct thrombin inhibitor and is a recommended first-line agent for the treatment of HIT. It is crucial to start alternative anticoagulation promptly due to the very high risk of further thrombosis.

  • ❌ Switch to unfractionated heparin infusion This is incorrect and dangerous. The antibodies that cause HIT cross- react between low-molecular-weight heparin (like the enoxaparin this patient received) and unfractionated heparin. Continuing any form of heparin would exacerbate the underlying pathological process, leading to further platelet activation and an increased risk of thrombosis. All heparin products, including line flushes, must be ceased immediately.
  • ❌ Commence warfarin Starting warfarin as monotherapy in the acute phase of HIT is contraindicated. Warfarin initially depletes the vitamin K-dependent anticoagulant proteins C and S more rapidly than the procoagulant factors (II, VII, IX, X). This can create a transient hypercoagulable state, paradoxically increasing the risk of thrombosis and potentially causing venous limb gangrene. Warfarin should only be considered once the platelet count has recovered and the patient is stable on an alternative anticoagulant.
  • ❌ Administer platelet transfusion Platelet transfusion is generally contraindicated in HIT unless the patient has life-threatening bleeding. Transfusing platelets can provide more substrate for the pathogenic antibody-platelet complexes, effectively 'fuelling the fire' and potentially worsening the prothrombotic state. The primary problem in HIT is thrombosis, not bleeding, despite the low platelet count.
  • ❌ Request anti-platelet factor 4 antibody test While this is the key investigation to confirm the diagnosis of HIT, it is not the most appropriate immediate management step. Treatment should not be delayed pending the results of this test, which can take several days to return. Clinical suspicion, often guided by a scoring system like the 4Ts score (which would be high in this patient), is sufficient to warrant immediate cessation of heparin and initiation of an alternative anticoagulant.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Flecainide is a class Ic sodium-channel blocker — contraindicated in structural heart disease and after myocardial infarction, where suppressing ectopy paradoxically increased mortality.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D048 — Cardiology · Hyperlipidaemia
questions.questionStem: What is the most important investigation to perform before commencing this medication?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 65-year-old man presents to the acute medical unit with a 12-hour history of palpitations. He has a history of hypertension. An ECG confirms atrial fibrillation with no acute ischaemic changes. A decision is made to pursue a rhythm control strategy with flecainide.

🩺 Examination:

His observations are stable with a heart rate of 130 bpm, irregularly irregular, and blood pressure of 145/88 mmHg.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
Transthoracic echocardiogram is the correct answer. Flecainide is a class Ic antiarrhythmic agent used for rhythm control in atrial fibrillation. A major contraindication to its use is the presence of structural or ischaemic heart disease. The CAST trial demonstrated increased mortality in patients with a history of myocardial infarction who were treated with flecainide. It is negatively inotropic and pro-arrhythmic in the context of a damaged myocardium. Therefore, UK guidelines mandate that structural heart disease must be excluded via an echocardiogram before flecainide is initiated. This patient's age and history of hypertension place him at risk of structural heart abnormalities like left ventricular hypertrophy.

  • ❌ CT pulmonary angiogram is an investigation to consider in a patient presenting with new-onset atrial fibrillation and breathlessness, as a pulmonary embolism can be a trigger. However, in this haemodynamically stable patient, it is not the most critical investigation required specifically before the administration of flecainide. The immediate priority is to ensure the chosen treatment is safe.
  • ❌ Serum troponin T would be a reasonable investigation as part of the general workup for a new arrhythmia, as myocardial ischaemia can be a precipitant. However, the ECG shows no acute ischaemic changes, making an acute coronary syndrome less likely. More importantly, it does not provide the structural information about the heart that is essential for the safe prescription of flecainide.
  • ❌ Thyroid function tests are a key part of the workup for any patient with new-onset atrial fibrillation, as thyrotoxicosis is an important and reversible cause. While this is a necessary investigation, it is not the most critical safety check required immediately prior to starting flecainide. The risk of pro-arrhythmia from flecainide in the context of structural heart disease is a more immediate danger.
  • ❌ 24-hour ambulatory ECG is used to diagnose paroxysmal arrhythmias or to assess arrhythmia burden over time. In this patient, atrial fibrillation has already been diagnosed on a 12-lead ECG, so a 24-hour monitor is not required at this stage and would not influence the immediate decision to commence flecainide.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Atorvastatin 20 mg for primary prevention when the 10-year QRISK3 score is ≥10%; atorvastatin 80 mg for established cardiovascular disease.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D049 — Cardiology · Hypertension in pregnancy
questions.questionStem: What would you advise?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 40-year-old man is referred by his GP for advice with regard to primary prevention of cardiovascular disease. He is a smoker with a strong family history of premature death from ischaemic heart disease. Following a period of lifestyle modification, his fasting cholesterol concentration is 7.2 mmol/litre. On consultation of the local guidelines you find that his estimated 10-year risk of a coronary heart disease event is > 30%.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
Prevention of cardiovascular disease

The Joint British Societies (JBS) for the Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease have recently updated their guidelines for managing lipids. Non-fasting blood samples should be taken to measure total cholesterol (TC) and HDL-cholesterol. In the past, fast LDLc was used, but a more pragmatic approach of measuring non-HDL-c is now being proposed (determined by TC minus HDL-c = non-HDL-c).

All high-risk people should receive professional lifestyle support to reduce total and LDL-c, raise HDL-c and lower triglycerides to reduce their CVD risk.

Individuals should be offered interventions to address all modifiable risk factors, including:

dietary advice

smoking cessation advice and support moderation of alcohol consumption weight reduction where appropriate.

The risk of patients should be determined by levels recommended by NICE: a number of different algorithms and risk predictors are available. NICE currently recommends QRISK2 for all primary prevention up to the age of 84 years. The JBS have also produced risk calculators.

Specific cholesterol-lowering drug therapy is recommended in: patients with established CVD individuals at particularly high risk of CVD: diabetes age > 40 years, patients with CKD stages 3–5, or FH individuals with high 10-year CVD risk – from the 2014 guidelines this is considered to be those with ≥10% chance of CVD within the next 10 years (previously this was 30%) individuals with high lifetime CVD risk estimated from heart age and other JBS3 calculator metrics, in whom lifestyle changes alone are considered insufficient by the physician and person concerned.

Statins are recommended as they are highly effective at reducing CVD events with evidence of benefit to LDL-c levels < 2 mmol/litre, which justifies intensive non-HDL-c lowering.

Statins are the most effective therapies in lowering cholesterol levels of the options listed. Therefore, it is the correct answer.

Total cholesterol levels of < 5 and LDL levels < 3 should be targeted for all primary prevention; in secondary prevention, < 4 and < 2, respectively.

Statins are safe, with trial evidence showing no effects on non-cardiovascular mortality or cancer. There is a small increase in risk of developing diabetes but the benefits of cholesterol lowering greatly exceed any risk associated with diabetes. If statin intolerance develops, a stepwise strategy involving switching agents and re- dosing is recommended. Despite low HDL-c levels contributing to CVD risk, drug therapy to raise HDL has not been shown to reduce CVD risk and is not currently indicated.

Hyperlipidaemia

Note on current guidance: NICE NG238 (which replaced CG181) specifies QRISK3 rather than QRISK2 for primary prevention risk estimation. The 10% ten-year threshold for offering atorvastatin 20 mg is unchanged.

  • ❌ A. Cholestyramine — Cholestyramine is incorrect. Cholestryamine is used in truly statin-intolerant patients and therefore is not the correct answer.
  • ❌ B. Dietician advice — Dietician advice is incorrect. He has already had a patient life-style modification and therefore dietician advice is not the best answer here.
  • ❌ C. Fibrate — Fibrate is incorrect. Fibrates have limited impact on cholesterol levels.
  • ❌ D. Nicotinic acid — Nicotinic acid is incorrect. Nicotinic acid is now unavailable for clinic use.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Labetalol is first-line, then nifedipine, then methyldopa. Women at high risk of pre-eclampsia take aspirin 75–150 mg daily from 12 weeks until birth.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D050 — Cardiology · Jugular venous pulse
questions.questionStem: Which one of the following interventions should be offered to reduce the risk of developing pre-eclampsia again?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

You review a 34-year-old woman who is 13 weeks pregnant. During her previous pregnancy she developed pre-eclampsia and had to have a caesarean section at 36 weeks gestation. Her blood pressure both following the last pregnancy and today is normal.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
The correct answer is low-dose aspirin. Low-dose aspirin (75-150 mg daily) has been shown to reduce the risk of developing pre-eclampsia in women at high risk, such as those with a history of pre-eclampsia in a previous pregnancy. According to the UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines, low-dose aspirin should be offered from 12 weeks gestation until the birth of the baby for women at high risk of developing pre-eclampsia.

Prophylactic nifedipine therapy and prophylactic labetalol therapy are not recommended for preventing pre-eclampsia. Nifedipine and labetalol are both antihypertensive medications that can be used to manage hypertension during pregnancy, but they have not been proven effective in reducing the risk of pre-eclampsia when used prophylactically.

Vitamin B6 supplementation has not been demonstrated to prevent pre-eclampsia either. Vitamin B6 is sometimes recommended for managing nausea and vomiting during pregnancy, but it does not have a role in preventing pre-eclampsia.

Finally, extended folic acid supplementation is not indicated for reducing the risk of pre-eclampsia. Folic acid supplementation is important during early pregnancy to reduce the risk of neural tube defects, but it does not have an established role in preventing pre- eclampsia. In the UK, folic acid supplementation is recommended until 12 weeks gestation.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Reading the JVP waveform:

  • a wave — atrial contraction; absent in atrial fibrillation, giant in tricuspid stenosis or pulmonary hypertension
  • Cannon a waves — atrium contracting against a closed tricuspid valve (complete heart block, ventricular tachycardia)
  • Giant v waves — tricuspid regurgitation
  • Steep y descent — constrictive pericarditis; absent y descent — tamponade

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D051 — Cardiology · Acute coronary syndrome
questions.questionStem: With regard to the JVP waveform, which of these features would you expect to see?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 68-year-old gentleman is brought into resus in your local emergency department after a syncopal episode. He is alert but clearly distressed. A formal ECG subsequently confirms that the arrhythmia is a ventricular tachycardia (VT) with a QRS complex duration of 150ms.

🩺 Examination:

The monitor above the bed showed a heart rate of 190bpm with a blood pressure of 85/50mmHg. His oxygen saturations are 98% in high flow oxygen (15L per minute via non-rebreathe mask). You are awaiting a full 12 lead ECG to be performed but the trace on cardiac monitor appears to show a regular broad complex tachycardia.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
The correct answer is B: cannon a waves.

Cannon a waves result from atrial contraction against a closed tricuspid valve and therefore can be seen in VT when atrial and ventricular contraction is not co-ordinated. They can also be seen in complete/3rd degree heart block and atrial flutter for the same reason.

Giant V waves are a features of tricuspid regurgitation; prominent x descent is a feature of constrictive pericarditis; slow y descent is a feature of cardiac tamponade and tricuspid stenosis; and large a waves can be found in tricuspid stenosis, right heart failure and pulmonary hypertension.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

In unstable angina or NSTEMI, risk stratify with a score predicting 6-month mortality (such as GRACE): predicted mortality above 3% means considering angiography with follow-on PCI within 72 hours.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D052 — Cardiology · Aortic stenosis
questions.questionStem: What would be the optimal management of the underlying cause of his chest pain besides usual medical measures?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 72-year-old diabetic man is admitted to the Emergency Department with a 40-min history of central chest pain. The pain eases after an hour with bed rest.

🔬 Investigations:

ECG shows mild anterior ST flattening. The troponin T level is slightly raised.

#MRCP #Question

options.text: Discharge home with referral to the outpatients department

questions.explanationHtml:
This patient falls into the high-risk category of acute coronary syndrome, an NSTEMI; although there are insufficient data to calculate a GRACE score, it is clear that further invasive investigations are required. Patients with NSTEMI that are invasively managed had improved prognosis than those managed medically. Furthermore, although the immediate risk of death in NSTEMI is lower than that of STEMI during the initial inpatient stay, the prognosis over the next year is actually much worse. Therefore, aggressive management is appropriate, particularly when significant ECG.

High-risk patients may have one or more of the following features: prolonged, ongoing (> 20 min) rest pain pulmonary oedema or angina with hypotension rest angina with dynamic ST changes > 1 mm raised troponin (I and T) age > 70 years diabetes mellitus.

Those at high risk should proceed to inpatient angiography with a view to proceeding to revascularisation, where appropriate, during that admission, so the inpatient coronary angiography is the best option.

  • ❌ A. Discharge home with referral to the outpatients department — Discharge home with referral to the outpatients department is incorrect. As described those at high risk should proceed to inpatient angiography with a view to proceeding to revascularisation, where appropriate, during that admission.
  • ❌ B. Exercise tolerance testing — Exercise tolerance testing (ETT) is incorrect. This is typically contraindicated in patients with a troponin rise and significant resting ECG changes.
  • ❌ D. IV abciximab infusion — IV abciximab infusion is incorrect. This would be considered if there was ongoing unstable chest pain at rest as a bridge to angiography. This is now rarely performed as access to angiography has improved dramatically.
  • ❌ E. Thrombolysis with tissue plasminogen activator — Thrombolysis with tissue plasminogen activator (TPA) is incorrect. This would only be suitable for STEMI in which PPCI was not available in a timely fashion (PPCI should be performed in STEMI within 2 h of arrival at the hospital). In this case, the diagnosis is NSTEMI and therefore TPA is not appropriate.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Age points to the cause: under 65 it is usually a bicuspid aortic valve; over 65 it is calcific degeneration. Rheumatic disease almost always affects the mitral valve too.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D053 — Cardiology · Murmurs
questions.questionStem: What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 53-year-old man is reviewed in the cardiology clinic with a history of chest pain and syncope.

🩺 Examination:

On examination he has an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotid area.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
The correct answer is Bicuspid aortic valve. This is the most likely cause of the patient's symptoms based on the clinical presentation. The patient presents with chest pain and syncope, which are classic symptoms of aortic stenosis. The ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotid area is characteristic of aortic stenosis. Bicuspid aortic valve is the most common congenital cardiac anomaly, affecting 1-2% of the population, and is the most common cause of aortic stenosis in patients under 65 years of age. A bicuspid aortic valve has two leaflets instead of the normal three, which predisposes to early calcification and stenosis. Patients with bicuspid aortic valves typically develop symptoms in their 50s or 60s, which aligns with this 53-year-old patient's presentation. The classic triad of symptoms in aortic stenosis includes angina (chest pain), syncope, and heart failure, though not all patients will exhibit all three symptoms.

  • ❌ Aortic root abscess is incorrect. An aortic root abscess is a serious complication of infective endocarditis, particularly involving the aortic valve. Patients typically present with fever, new or changing heart murmurs, and signs of systemic infection. The absence of fever or other signs of infection in this case makes an aortic root abscess unlikely. Additionally, aortic root abscesses often cause conduction abnormalities due to their proximity to the conduction system, which was not mentioned in this case.
  • ❌ Post rheumatic fever is incorrect. While rheumatic fever can lead to valvular heart disease, including aortic stenosis, it typically affects the mitral valve more commonly than the aortic valve. Rheumatic aortic stenosis usually presents later in life than bicuspid aortic valve disease and is becoming increasingly rare in developed countries due to the effective treatment of streptococcal infections. Additionally, patients with rheumatic heart disease often have a history of rheumatic fever in childhood, which was not mentioned in this case.
  • ❌ Posterior myocardial infarction is incorrect. While a posterior myocardial infarction can cause chest pain, it would not typically cause a systolic murmur radiating to the carotids. Posterior myocardial infarctions may be associated with mitral regurgitation due to papillary muscle dysfunction, which would produce a pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla, not an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids. Additionally, syncope is not a typical presenting symptom of myocardial infarction unless there are significant conduction abnormalities or cardiogenic shock.
  • ❌ Calcification of the aortic valve is incorrect as a standalone diagnosis, although it is part of the pathophysiology. Calcific aortic stenosis is indeed a common cause of aortic stenosis in older patients (typically over 65 years), but it is usually degenerative in nature and affects a previously normal trileaflet valve. In younger patients like this 53-year- old man, aortic stenosis is more commonly due to a congenital bicuspid aortic valve that has undergone accelerated calcification. While calcification is the process that leads to stenosis, the underlying anatomical abnormality (bicuspid valve) is the primary cause in this age group.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Dynamic manoeuvres separate murmurs:

  • Inspiration accentuates right-sided murmurs; expiration accentuates left-sided ones (RILE)
  • Valsalva and standing reduce preload — softens most murmurs but intensifies hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy and mitral valve prolapse
  • Squatting and handgrip raise afterload — intensifies mitral and aortic regurgitation, softens the obstructive cardiomyopathy murmur

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D054 — Cardiology · Angina pectoris
questions.questionStem: Which one of the following conditions is most associated with this kind of murmur?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 66-year-old man presents with shortness-of-breath on exertion.

🩺 Examination:

On examination his blood pressure is 128/76 mmHg, pulse 78 / min and regular. Auscultation of his chest reveals an early diastolic murmur.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
The correct answer is Aortic regurgitation. An early diastolic murmur is characteristic of aortic regurgitation, which occurs when the aortic valve does not close properly, allowing blood to flow back into the left ventricle during diastole. This can be due to various causes such as degeneration of the valve, endocarditis, or aortic root dilation. The murmur is best heard at the left sternal edge in the second intercostal space with the patient sitting up and leaning forward.

Atrial septal defect is incorrect because this condition typically presents with a systolic ejection murmur rather than an early diastolic murmur. An atrial septal defect is a congenital heart defect where there is an opening between the atria, leading to the shunting of blood from left to right. This results in increased pulmonary blood flow and volume overload on the right side of the heart.

Mitral stenosis is also incorrect as it presents with a mid-diastolic murmur rather than an early diastolic murmur. Mitral stenosis occurs when the mitral valve narrows and obstructs blood flow from the left atrium to the left ventricle during diastole. This can be caused by rheumatic heart disease or other less common etiologies such as congenital abnormalities or infective endocarditis.

Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM) is not associated with an early diastolic murmur either. HOCM presents with a harsh systolic ejection murmur that increases in intensity during the Valsalva manoeuvre or standing up quickly from a squatting position. This condition involves hypertrophy of the interventricular septum, which can obstruct blood flow out of the left ventricle during systole.

Finally, Mitral regurgitation is an incorrect option as it presents with a pansystolic murmur rather than an early diastolic murmur. Mitral regurgitation occurs when the mitral valve does not close properly during systole, allowing blood to flow back into the left atrium. This can be caused by various factors such as degeneration of the valve, rheumatic heart disease, or mitral valve prolapse.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

GTN advice patients are actually meant to be given: take a second dose after 5 minutes if pain persists, and call an ambulance if pain remains 5 minutes after that second dose.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D055 — Cardiology · Atrial fibrillation
questions.questionStem: What would be the next stage of treatment for this patient?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 68-year-old man presents to you with intermittent left-sided crushing chest pain which is brought on by walking his dog on an incline. The pain settles within a couple of minutes of rest and glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) spray. The pain is not associated with shortness of breath or lightheadedness. He first presented to you with these same symptoms six months ago, at this time you gave him lifestyle advice and prescribed bisoprolol, aspirin, GTN and atorvastatin. He has noted only minimal improvement of his symptoms over the last six months.

🩺 Examination:

On examination he is comfortable at rest, with blood pressure 124/73 mmHg, heart rate 63 beats/minute, oxygen saturation 99%, respiratory rate 18 breaths/minute and he is afebrile. His chest is clear, and heart sounds are normal.

🔬 Investigations:

ECG shows normal sinus rhythm, with no ischaemic changes. He is also awaiting a CT coronary angiography.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
If monotherapy with bisoprolol has not been successful, the next step in treating stable angina is to add a long-acting dihydropyridine calcium- channel blocker, such as amlodipine.

Bisoprolol should not be given concurrently with a non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker, like verapamil, as both reduce conduction at the AV node and this could lead to complete heart block.

A long-acting nitrate or nicorandil might be considered if an additional calcium channel blocker was not tolerated. But this would not be a second-line treatment plan.

As a side note, the maximum dose of bisoprolol within 24 hours is typically 10mg, and although higher doses are sometimes prescribed by cardiologists, this would not be the most appropriate next step, especially considering his low-normal heart rate of 63 beats per minute.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Atrial fibrillation of more than 48 hours' duration, going for rhythm control: delay cardioversion until therapeutic anticoagulation has been maintained for at least 3 weeks, offering rate control meanwhile.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D056 — Cardiology · Mitral stenosis
questions.questionStem: Which one of the following reasons could be responsible for the delay?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 68-year-old man with AF is admitted electively for DC cardioversion (DCCV), to be performed as a day-case procedure. However, the procedure is postponed to a later date.

#MRCP #Question

options.text: He had discontinued digoxin for the last 2 days
His serum potassium level was 4.2 mEq/l
He had an episode of angina 2 days ago

questions.explanationHtml:
The international normalised ratio (INR) should be above 2.0 not only on the day of the procedure, but also during the preceding 3–4 weeks. An alternative is to perform a transoesophageal echocardiogram on the day of the procedure to check for clot; however, four weeks of effective anti-coagulation post-procedure will still be required (due to atrial stunning – where despite sinus rhythm, the mechanical function of the atrium is not fully restored). Cardioversion External cardioversion is a safe and effective method for restoring sinus rhythm, and should be attempted at least once in every patient with chronic atrial fibrillation (AF) Overt congestive heart failure, hypokalaemia and hyperthyroidism should be controlled as much as possible before cardioversion Acute myocardial infarction is not a contraindication to cardioversion If the patient has a slow ventricular response of AF in the absence of anti-arrhythmic drugs, cardioversion should be performed after the insertion of a temporary transvenous-pacing catheter.

Success

Electrical cardioversion is initially successful in 70–94% cases, but relapse is frequent (25–50% at one month and 70–90% at one year) The success depends on the duration of AF, transthoracic impedance, left atrial size and the age of the patient Antero-posterior positioning of the paddles is more often successful than the usual thoracic positioning.

Procedure

The initial shock strength should be 100 J, followed by a second 200-J shock and a third 360-J shock If AF persists, a second 360-J shock with the paddles in the anteroposterior position can be attempted Shocks must be synchronised with the R-wave to avoid R-on-T phenomena and Torsardes de Pointes. Some machines require ‘sync’ to be pressed manually for every shock Immediate DC cardioversion, after the administration of intravenous heparin or subcutaneous LMWH, is appropriate in an emergency or if AF has been present for less than 48 hours Anticoagulation should be continued for at least 4 weeks after successful cardioversion.

  • ❌ A. He had discontinued digoxin for the last 2 days — He had discontinued digoxin for the last two days is incorrect. Typically digoxin is stopped on the day of the procedure, as it was thought that digoxin therapy with DCCV predisposed to ventricular arrhythmias. If there is evidence of digoxin toxicity this must be corrected before DCCV.
  • ❌ B. He was taking amiodarone — He was taking amiodarone is incorrect. Pre-treatment with amiodarone or sotalol may prevent early recurrence.
  • ❌ D. His serum potassium level was 4.2 mEq/l — His serum potassium level was 4.2 mEq/l is incorrect. A normal potassium level does not preclude DCCV.
  • ❌ E. He had an episode of angina 2 days ago — He had an episode of angina 2 days ago is incorrect. A history of angina does not preclude DCCV. 41866

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Mitral stenosis — almost always rheumatic:

  • Malar flush, atrial fibrillation, haemoptysis
  • Loud S1 (leaflets still wide open at end-diastole), opening snap, low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble with presystolic accentuation in sinus rhythm
  • A shorter S2-to-opening-snap interval means higher left atrial pressure and more severe stenosis

The large left atrium causes hoarseness by compressing the recurrent laryngeal nerve (Ortner's syndrome).

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D057 — Cardiology · Heart failure
questions.questionStem: What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 25-year-old woman is seen in the outpatients department and found to have a loud first heart sound, an early diastole sound, followed by a mid-diastolic murmur. She tells you that when she was a child, she had a non- specific illness which her doctor at the time thought may be rheumatic fever, but which was never proven by biochemical testing.

#MRCP #Question

options.text: Mitral stenosis with a fourth heart sound

questions.explanationHtml:
There is a loud first heart sound and, if an opening ‘snap’ is heard, this indicates that the mitral valve is mobile (‘mobile leaflets’). The snap occurs if the superior systolic bowing of the anterior mitral valve leaflet is reversed rapidly towards the left ventricle in early diastole, owing to the high left atrial pressure.

  • ❌ A. Mitral stenosis with a fourth heart sound — Mitral stenosis with a fourth heart sound is incorrect. There is no mention of a fourth heart sound. The latter is often associated with filling of a stiff left ventricle (this can be seen in left ventricular hypertrophy, amyloid, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, or scarred/fibrosed left ventricle due to ischaemia). The fourth heart sound is classically late diastolic or presystolic. It occurs if augmented atrial contraction causes presystolic ventricular distension so that the ventricle contracts with greater force.
  • ❌ B. Mitral stenosis with atrial fibrillation — Mitral stenosis with atrial fibrillation is incorrect. There is mention of an irregularly irregular pulse (atrial fibrillation). Atrial fibrillation often is associated with a variable first heart sound.
  • ❌ D. Mitral stenosis with pulmonary hypertension — Mitral stenosis with pulmonary hypertension is incorrect. Pulmonary hypertension is associated with an accentuated pulmonary component of the second heart sound, a right ventricular third heart sound, and parasternal heave indicating a hypertrophied left atrium.
  • ❌ E. Mitral valve prolapse — Mitral valve prolapse is incorrect. Mitral valve prolapse is associated with a mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur heard best at the apex. Important associations to be aware of: ‘Soft first heart sound (S1)’: immobile mitral stenosis, hypodynamic state, mitral regurgitation, long PR interval ‘Split S1’: right bundle branch block, left bundle branch block, ventricular tachycardia, Ebstein’s anomaly ‘Variable S1’: atrial fibrillation, complete heart block ‘Loud S2’: hypertension, tachycardia, atrial septal defect ‘Soft/absent S2’: severe aortic stenosis ‘Fixed splitting S2’: atrial septal defect ‘Wide split S2’: right bundle branch block, pulmonary stenosis, mitral regurgitation ‘Single S2’: severe pulmonary stenosis, aortic stenosis, hypertension, ventricular septal defect, tetralogy of Fallot, Eisenmenger’s syndrome ‘Reversed split S2’: left bundle branch block, right ventricular pacing, patent ductus arteriosus, aortic stenosis ‘S3’: rapid left ventricular filling (mitral regurgitation, ventricular septal defect), can be normal in children ‘S4’: filling of stiff left ventricle (left ventricular hypertrophy, amyloid, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, ischaemia).

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Loop diuretics relieve congestion but do not improve survival — they are titrated up and down to symptoms, and are never the prognostic part of the regimen.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D058 — Cardiology · Hypertension
questions.questionStem: Which one of the following drugs should be added to his list of medications with respect to his overall prognosis?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 60-year-old White man, with NYHA (New York Heart Association) class II heart failure, is taking an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors and bisoprolol for his heart failure. He is also taking 50 mg of furosemide. He is generally well in himself. On direct questioning at his routine outpatient visit, he has noticed a severe deterioration in his exercise tolerance over the last year and he now sleeps in a chair downstairs because he finds it impossible to climb the stairs owing to shortness of breath.

🩺 Examination:

Examination reveals a blood pressure of 105/72 mmHg, pulse of 85 bpm and regular. There are bilateral basal crackles on auscultation of the chest, and bilateral ankle swelling.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
The European Society of Cardiology recommends the addition of spironolactone for improving the survival of patients who are in the transition from well-controlled class II to class III or IV heart failure; the mortality benefit is considerable. Given that the patient is having a worsening of symptoms despite ACE-I and beta blocker, spironolactone is the next most appropriate therapy for prognosis.

  • ❌ A. Digoxin — Digoxin is incorrect. Digoxin helps to relieve symptoms to some extent, and is more useful if the patient is in atrial fibrillation; however, there is no overt prognostic benefit with digoxin and, therefore, it is not the correct answer.
  • ❌ B. Bumetanide — Bumetanide is incorrect. Diuretics are only indicated if there is fluid retention and are associated with a worse prognosis overall; it is recommended that they are stopped if it is safe to do so when the patient is euvolaemic.
  • ❌ C. Isosorbide mononitrate — Isosorbide mononitrate is incorrect. Nitrates and hydralazine in combination help to improve symptoms in patients with class III and IV heart failure.
  • ❌ E. Valsartan — Valsartan is incorrect. Combinations of ACE-inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers are no longer recommended in the majority of patients as hyperkalaemia, hypotension and impaired renal function are more likely. There are some data that ACE-inhibitors and ARBs together improve prognosis for a select group of heart failure patients, but safety concerns remain.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Step 1 depends on age and ethnicity: under 55 and not of black African or African-Caribbean family origin → ACE inhibitor or ARB; aged 55 or over, or of black African or African-Caribbean origin → calcium channel blocker.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D059 — Cardiology · Patent ductus arteriosus
questions.questionStem: What is the most suitable choice of medication to add to control his blood pressure from the list below?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 55-year-old man presents to his general practitioner for an annual blood pressure review. He has a past medical history of essential hypertension and takes amlodipine. He does not smoke cigarettes or drink alcohol. He is originally from Somalia and is of Black African ethnicity. A recent ambulatory blood pressure monitoring reading demonstrates an average blood pressure of 165/93 mmHg.

🩺 Examination:

The examination is unremarkable.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
Losartan is the correct answer. Options in step two of the NICE hypertension management guideline include the addition of a thiazide diuretic, ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB). ACE inhibitors are less effective in ethnically black populations and therefore ARB medications are recommended in their place in this population.

  • ❌ Atenolol is incorrect. This is a possible option for treatment of hypertension but is typically reserved for those patients with refractory hypertension on a combination of calcium channel blockers, ACE inhibitors (or ARBs) and thiazide diuretics.
  • ❌ Doxazosin is incorrect. This is a possible option for treatment of hypertension but is typically reserved for those patients with refractory hypertension on a combination of calcium channel blockers, ACE inhibitors (or ARBs) and thiazide diuretics.
  • ❌ Ramipril is incorrect. ACE inhibitors are less effective in patients of Black African origin.
  • ❌ Spironolactone is incorrect. This is a possible option for treatment of hypertension but is typically reserved for those patients with refractory hypertension on a combination of calcium channel blockers, ACE inhibitors (or ARBs) and thiazide diuretics. K+ should be < 4.5 when commencing.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Continuous 'machinery' murmur below the left clavicle. Indometacin or ibuprofen close the duct by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis; prostaglandin E keeps it open when the circulation is duct-dependent.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D060 — Cardiology · Infective endocarditis
questions.questionStem: Which of the following drugs can treat the underlying condition of the newborn baby if the symptoms persist after one week?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 35-year-old female delivers a newborn at 30 weeks of gestation. During the first trimester, the mother suffered from fever and joint pain for one week. At that time, she only received symptomatic treatment. Today, the patient delivered a premature baby via normal vaginal delivery.

🩺 Examination:

On examination of the newborn continuous machine-like murmur is heard in the left infraclavicular space.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
This newborn is suffering from patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), a non- cyanotic congenital heart disorder. It is a type of left-to-right shunt in which blood passes from the aorta to the pulmonary vessel via the patent ductus arteriosus. Newborns may have a normal presentation, but on auscultation, a continuous machine-like murmur is characteristic. Indomethacin or ibuprofen is used for treating the patent ductus arteriosus in a newborn.

  • ❌ Indapamide is a thiazide diuretic. It does not treat patent ductus arteriosus.
  • ❌ Mifepristone is an anti-progesterone drug. It is used along with misoprostol to terminate labour. It does not close the patent ductus arteriosus.
  • ❌ Progesterone is a sex hormone in females. It does not close the patent ductus arteriosus.
  • ❌ Prostaglandins can keep the ductus arteriosus open. They are used to keep the ductus arteriosus open in cyanotic disorders like transposition of great vessels (TGA) until the definitive surgery is performed.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Organism points to the setting:

  • Staphylococcus aureus — commonest overall, and in intravenous drug use (right-sided, tricuspid)
  • Staphylococcus epidermidis — prosthetic valve endocarditis within the first year
  • Viridans streptococci — subacute disease after dental procedures
  • Streptococcus gallolyticus (bovis) — investigate the colon for malignancy
  • Culture-negative — prior antibiotics, Coxiella, Bartonella, HACEK organisms

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D061 — Cardiology · Peri-arrest rhythms
questions.questionStem: What pathogen is most likely to be responsible for this patient's illness?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 65-year-old male patient presents with a 3-week history of fatigue, generalised weakness, and subjective fevers. The patient's past medical history is notable for rheumatic heart disease and COPD. He reports no recent travel or unwell contacts, and reports no intravenous drug use. Last year, he had a screening colonoscopy which was unremarkable. Preliminary results from blood cultures reveal gram-positive cocci.

🩺 Examination:

On physical exam, he is noted to have very poor dental hygiene with gingivitis, splinter haemorrhages, a pansystolic murmur and a mid- diastolic, rumbling murmur heard loudest at the 5th intercostal space and mid-axillary line.

🔬 Investigations:

An echocardiogram reveals a vegetation on the mitral valve with moderate mitral regurgitation and mitral stenosis.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
The vignette describes a patient with subacute bacterial endocarditis (SBE) which is usually caused by viridans streptococci, such as Streptococcus sanguinis, which are commonly found as oral flora. Poor dental hygiene, particularly in the setting of gingival disease, is a risk factor for the development of SBE. Unlike acute bacterial endocarditis which can affect healthy native valves, the viridans streptococci typically affect prosthetic valves or damaged heart valves and follows a more indolent (subacute) clinical course. In this case, the patient's rheumatic heart disease predisposed him to develop SBE affecting the diseased mitral valve.

Acute bacterial endocarditis is typically caused by Staphylococcus aureus. The presence of indwelling lines, particularly in combination with prosthetic heart valves and/or pacemaker leads, can provide a seeding nidus of infection for Staphylococcus epidermidis - a common skin commensal.

Streptococcus bovis endocarditis has been associated with colon cancer, with some cross-sectional data to suggest that 33-50% of patients with Strep bovis bacteraemia and/or endocarditis have a colorectal adenoma or carcinoma on subsequent colonoscopy. The patient's normal colonoscopy the year prior makes this a less likely cause.

Finally, beta-hemolytic streptococci, such as Streptococcus pyogenes, are an uncommon cause of infective endocarditis.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Adverse features — shock, syncope, myocardial ischaemia, heart failure — turn any tachyarrhythmia into an electrical problem: synchronised DC cardioversion, up to three attempts, before drugs.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D062 — Cardiology · Pre-eclampsia
questions.questionStem: What is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 68-year-old man is admitted to the Acute Medical Unit with palpitations. He has a history of ischaemic heart disease. He is alert and has no chest pain.

🩺 Examination:

His blood pressure is 134/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation is 97% on room air.

🔬 Investigations:

An ECG shows a regular broad complex tachycardia at a rate of 160 beats/min.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
IV amiodarone is the correct answer. This patient is presenting with a regular broad complex tachycardia (BCT). According to the Resuscitation Council (UK) guidelines, the management of any tachycardia is dictated by the presence or absence of adverse (unstable) features. This patient is haemodynamically stable, with a normal blood pressure, adequate oxygen saturation, and no signs of shock, syncope, myocardial ischaemia, or heart failure. For a stable, regular BCT, the rhythm should be presumed to be ventricular tachycardia (VT) until proven otherwise, especially in a patient with a history of ischaemic heart disease. The first- line pharmacological treatment for stable VT is an intravenous loading dose of amiodarone. This is the safest and most effective initial approach in this undifferentiated BCT scenario.

  • ❌ IV adenosine is incorrect. Adenosine is the first-line treatment for a stable, regular, narrow-complex tachycardia (i.e., supraventricular tachycardia, SVT). It works by causing transient AV nodal block, which can terminate re-entrant tachycardias involving the AV node. While it can occasionally be used as a diagnostic tool in BCT if SVT with aberrant conduction is strongly suspected, it is not the recommended first-line treatment for an undifferentiated regular BCT. Administering adenosine to a patient with VT can be ineffective and, in some cases, may cause haemodynamic deterioration or acceleration of the arrhythmia.
  • ❌ IV metoprolol is not the most appropriate initial choice. While beta- blockers are used for rate control in some tachyarrhythmias (e.g., atrial fibrillation), they are not the first-line therapy for stable, undifferentiated regular BCT. In a patient with presumed VT, particularly with a background of ischaemic heart disease, there is a risk of underlying impaired left ventricular function. The negative inotropic effects of beta- blockers could precipitate haemodynamic collapse in this situation. Therefore, amiodarone is preferred as the initial agent due to its more favourable safety profile in this context.
  • ❌ IV verapamil is incorrect and potentially dangerous. Verapamil, a non- dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, is strongly contraindicated in the management of an undifferentiated BCT. If the underlying rhythm is VT, administering verapamil can cause profound vasodilation and negative inotropy, leading to severe hypotension and cardiovascular collapse. This is a critical safety principle in arrhythmia management. Verapamil should only ever be considered if a diagnosis of SVT with aberrant conduction has been definitively confirmed, which is not the case in this scenario.
  • ❌ Synchronised DC cardioversion is the correct management for a patient with a BCT who is haemodynamically unstable. Adverse features indicating instability include shock (systolic BP < 90 mmHg), syncope, myocardial ischaemia (e.g., chest pain), or acute heart failure. This patient is explicitly described as being stable, with a blood pressure of 134/82 mmHg and no chest pain. As he is stable, immediate electrical cardioversion is not indicated, and pharmacological therapy should be the initial approach.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Aspirin 75–150 mg daily from 12 weeks is offered for one high-risk or two moderate-risk factors.

  • High risk: previous hypertensive disease in pregnancy, chronic kidney disease, autoimmune disease, type 1 or 2 diabetes, chronic hypertension
  • Moderate risk: first pregnancy, age ≥40, pregnancy interval >10 years, BMI ≥35 at booking, family history of pre-eclampsia, multiple pregnancy

Smoking is not a risk factor — it is consistently associated with lower risk.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D063 — Cardiology · Supraventricular tachycardia
questions.questionStem: Which one of the following is not a risk factor for the development of pre-eclampsia?
questions.explanationHtml:
The correct answer is Smoking. Contrary to most other health conditions, smoking has been shown in numerous studies not to be a risk factor for the development of pre-eclampsia. In fact, some research suggests that smoking may have a protective effect against pre- eclampsia, although this does not outweigh the various other harmful effects of smoking on both mother and baby.

The remaining options are all recognised risk factors for pre-eclampsia:

A Body mass index of 38 kg/m^2 is well into the obese range (a BMI of 30 or above is classified as obesity). Obesity is a known risk factor for pre-eclampsia, with the risk increasing as BMI increases. The mechanism behind this association isn't entirely understood but it's thought that obesity-related inflammation and endothelial dysfunction may play a role.

A woman carrying twins, or multiple pregnancies, significantly increases the risk of developing pre-eclampsia. This increased risk is due to two main factors: firstly, with more placental tissue there's greater opportunity for placental insufficiency to occur; secondly, women carrying multiples often have higher levels of hormones such as human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), which can contribute to the development of pre-eclampsia.

Nulliparity, or never having given birth before, is another well- established risk factor for pre-eclampsia. It's unclear why nulliparous women are at higher risk but it may be related to their immune system's response to pregnancy.

Finally, Diabetes mellitus, whether type 1 or type 2, significantly increases the likelihood of developing pre-eclampsia. This is likely due to a combination of factors including endothelial dysfunction caused by hyperglycaemia and possibly also insulin resistance. Diabetic women also often have other associated conditions such as hypertension and kidney disease which further increase their risk.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Adenosine causes bronchospasm — avoid it in asthma and use verapamil instead. Warn every patient about the transient chest tightness, flushing and sense of doom.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D064 — Cardiology · Pulmonary Hypertension
questions.questionStem: What is the most appropriate initial management step?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 28-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a 30- minute history of sudden-onset palpitations and light-headedness. She has no significant past medical history. An ECG confirms a regular, narrow complex tachycardia with no clearly discernible P waves.

🩺 Examination:

On examination, she is alert and her observations are: heart rate 180 bpm and blood pressure 115/75 mmHg.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
Valsalva manoeuvre is the correct answer. The patient is presenting with a regular narrow complex tachycardia and is haemodynamically stable (BP 115/75 mmHg, alert). According to the Resuscitation Council UK guidelines for supraventricular tachycardia (SVT), the initial management for a stable patient is to attempt vagal manoeuvres. The Valsalva manoeuvre is a safe, non-invasive, and often effective method to terminate the arrhythmia. It works by increasing intrathoracic pressure, which stimulates the vagus nerve, leading to increased parasympathetic tone. This slows conduction through the atrioventricular (AV) node, potentially breaking the re-entrant circuit responsible for most SVTs (like AVNRT). If this fails, then pharmacological therapy would be the next step.

  • ❌ Intravenous adenosine is an incorrect choice for the initial step. While it is the first-line pharmacological treatment for stable SVT, it should only be administered after vagal manoeuvres have been attempted and have failed. Adenosine is a very short-acting AV nodal blocking agent that is highly effective at terminating re-entrant tachycardias involving the AV node. However, due to its side-effect profile (including transient asystole, chest tightness, and bronchospasm), the non-invasive vagal manoeuvre should always be tried first in a stable patient.
  • ❌ Intravenous amiodarone is not a first-line agent for the acute management of stable, regular narrow complex tachycardia. Its primary role in tachyarrhythmias is in the management of broad complex tachycardias, atrial fibrillation (for rate or rhythm control), or in cases of SVT refractory to other treatments. Given its potential for significant side effects (e.g., hypotension, bradycardia, long-term organ toxicity), it is reserved for specific situations and would not be the initial choice here.
  • ❌ Intravenous verapamil, a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, is a second-line pharmacological agent for stable SVT. It can be used if adenosine is contraindicated (e.g., in patients with severe asthma or bronchospasm) or if both vagal manoeuvres and adenosine have failed to terminate the rhythm. It works by slowing conduction through the AV node but is not the most appropriate initial step in the management algorithm.
  • ❌ Synchronised DC cardioversion is the treatment of choice for patients with a tachyarrhythmia who are haemodynamically unstable. Signs of instability include shock (systolic BP <90 mmHg), syncope, severe heart failure, or evidence of myocardial ischaemia. This patient is alert with a normal blood pressure and is therefore considered stable. Using electrical cardioversion at this stage would be inappropriate and unnecessarily aggressive.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Five groups, five mechanisms:

  • 1 — pulmonary arterial hypertension (idiopathic, heritable, connective tissue disease, congenital shunts)
  • 2 — left heart disease (much the commonest)
  • 3 — lung disease and hypoxia
  • 4 — chronic thromboembolic disease
  • 5 — unclear or multifactorial (sarcoidosis, myeloproliferative disease)

Group 2 must be excluded before pulmonary vasodilators are considered.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D065 — Cardiology · Pulses
questions.questionStem: Which one of the following is the likely diagnosis?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 35-year-old woman gives a history of progressive exertional dyspnoea and fatigue over the last year. Pulmonary function testing rules out obstructive airways disease. ANCA and HIV testing are negative.

🩺 Examination:

Examination reveals features of right-sided heart failure with pulmonary hypertension, but there are no crackles to suggest fibrosis.

🔬 Investigations:

Lung perfusion scanning and pulmonary angiography fail to detect pulmonary thromboembolic disease. An echocardiogram shows enlarged right heart chambers.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
The symptoms, signs and echocardiographic features are consistent with pulmonary hypertension. The negative investigations suggest that the likely diagnosis is pulmonary arterial hypertension (primary or idiopathic pulmonary hypertension).

Pulmonary hypertension:

Pulmonary hypertension is a haemodynamic and pathophysiological state that is found in multiple clinical conditions It is characterised by a mean pulmonary artery pressure (PAP) 25 mmHg on right heart catheterisation The most recent clinical classification of pulmonary hypertension (Dana Point, 2008) divides it up into five groups Chat It is essential to differentiate the term 'pulmonary hypertension (PH)', which refers to an with AI Tutor elevation in the mean pulmonary artery pressure, from the term 'pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH)', which refers to a clinical condition characterised by pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension in the absence of other causes.

Pulmonary arterial hypertension (WHO Group 1):

Pulmonary arterial hypertension is a clinical condition characterised by pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension (ie with a low pulmonary wedge pressure < 15 mmHg) in the absence of any other possible cause of similar haemodynamic abnormalities Other texts may refer to it as primary or idiopathic pulmonary hypertension Pulmonary arterial hypertension secondary to congenital shunts is included in this category.

Pulmonary hypertension due to other causes:

WHO Group 2: Left heart disease From left ventricular dysfunction or valvular disease WHO Group 3: Lung disease or hypoxia Chronic lung disease such as COPD or ILD that lead to vasoconstriction due to chronic hypoxia WHO Group 4: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension

From pulmonary thromboembolic disease

WHO Group 5: Unclear or multifactorial mechanisms.

  • ❌ A. Pulmonary vasculitis — Pulmonary vasculitis is incorrect. It can also be associated with vasculitis, but this patient has a normal ANCA.
  • ❌ B. Mitral valve prolapse — Mitral valve prolapse is incorrect. Pulmonary hypertension can be caused by left heart disease, but this was not found on echocardiography of this patient.
  • ❌ D. Mitral stenosis — Mitral stenosis is incorrect. Pulmonary hypertension can be caused by left heart disease, but this was not found on echocardiography of this patient.
  • ❌ E. Dilated cardiomyopathy — Dilated cardiomyopathy is incorrect. Pulmonary hypertension can be caused by left heart disease, but this was not found on echocardiography of this patient.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Pulse character as a diagnosis:

  • Slow-rising — aortic stenosis
  • Collapsing — aortic regurgitation, patent ductus, thyrotoxicosis, anaemia
  • Pulsus bisferiens — mixed aortic valve disease
  • Pulsus paradoxus — tamponade, severe asthma
  • Pulsus alternans — severe left ventricular failure
  • Jerky — hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy

questions.name: D066 — Cardiology · Statins
questions.questionStem: An echocardiogram is performed in the clinic:
questions.questionHtml:
❓

An 84-year-old man presents with shortness of breath on exertion.

🩺 Examination:

On examination, you note bibasal crackles, pitting oedema to the mid calves, and an ejection systolic murmur.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
Bisferiens pulse is correct. Mixed aortic valve disease is associated with a bisferiens pulse. A bisferiens pulse is a specific type of arterial pulse waveform observed during palpation of the pulse at various pulse points in the body, typically the radial artery. This pulse is characterized by having two distinct systolic peaks separated by a mid-systolic dip. When both aortic regurgitation and aortic stenosis are present together, they can result in a bisferiens pulse pattern due to the complex interactions between the regurgitant and stenotic flows.

  • ❌ Collapsing pulse is incorrect. A collapsing pulse is associated with aortic regurgitation, patent ductus arteriosus and hyperkinetic states. Although the patient has aortic regurgitation, a bisferiens pulse is the best answer since the patient has mixed aortic valve disease.
  • ❌ Pulsus alternans is incorrect. Pulsus alterans is defined as the regular alternation of the force of the arterial pulse which is associated with severe left ventricular systolic (LVSD). Although the patient has LVSD, it is only mild, and pulsus alterans would therefore not be expected.
  • ❌ Pulsus paradoxus is incorrect. This is characterised by a faint or absent pulse on inspiration due to a fall in systolic blood pressure. It is associated with severe asthma and cardiac tamponade.
  • ❌ Slow-rising pulse is incorrect. This type of pulse is associated with aortic stenosis. Although the patient has aortic stenosis, a bisferiens pulse is the best answer since the patient has mixed aortic valve disease.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting step of hepatic cholesterol synthesis. Check liver enzymes at baseline, 3 months and 12 months; check creatine kinase only if there is unexplained muscle pain.

questions.name: D067 — Cardiology · Torsades de pointes
questions.questionStem: What is the most appropriate course of action?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 52-year-old man with a history of hypertension is found to have a 10- year cardiovascular disease risk of 28%. A decision is made to start atorvastatin 20mg on. Liver function tests are performed prior to initialising treatment: Three months later the LFTs are repeated:

🔬 Investigations:

Bilirubin 10 µmol/l (3 - 17 µmol/l)

ALP 96 u/l (30 - 150 u/l)

ALT 30 u/l (10 - 45 u/l)

Gamma-GT 28 u/l (10 - 40 u/l)

Bilirubin 12 µmol/l (3 - 17 µmol/l)

ALP 107 u/l (30 - 150 u/l)

ALT 104 u/l (10 - 45 u/l)

Gamma-GT 76 u/l (10 - 40 u/l)

#MRCP #Question

options.text: Continue treatment and repeat LFTs in 1 month
Reduce dose to atorvastatin 10mg on and repeat LFTs in 1 month
Stop treatment and consider alternative lipid lowering drug
Stop treatment and refer to gastroenterology

questions.correctAnswerText: Continue treatment and repeat LFTs in 1 month
questions.explanationHtml:
The correct answer is Continue treatment and repeat LFTs in 1 month. According to NICE guidelines, statins can be continued if ALT is raised but less than 3 times the upper limit of normal (ULN). In this case, the ALT is 104 u/l, which is approximately 2.3 times the ULN of 45 u/l. While there is a rise in liver enzymes, this is a common finding with statin therapy and often transient. The appropriate course is to continue the current dose and monitor LFTs after one month to ensure they don't rise further.

  • ❌ Check creatine kinase would be appropriate if the patient was presenting with muscle symptoms such as myalgia, but there is no mention of muscle symptoms in this scenario. Routine CK monitoring is not recommended in asymptomatic patients on statins.
  • ❌ Reduce dose to atorvastatin 10mg on and repeat LFTs in 1 month is unnecessary as the current elevation in liver enzymes is within acceptable limits for continuing the current dose. Dose reduction would only be considered if ALT was persistently elevated or exceeded 3 times ULN.
  • ❌ Stop treatment and consider alternative lipid lowering drug is too aggressive a response. The elevation in liver enzymes is modest and within acceptable limits. Discontinuing treatment would unnecessarily deprive the patient of the cardiovascular benefits of statin therapy, particularly given their high 10-year cardiovascular risk.
  • ❌ Stop treatment and refer to gastroenterology is inappropriate as the liver function abnormalities are mild and likely statin-related. Referral to gastroenterology would be considered if there were features suggesting significant liver disease or if ALT was persistently elevated above 3 times ULN despite stopping the statin.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Intravenous magnesium sulfate is the treatment for torsades de pointes — and amiodarone must be avoided, since prolonging the QT further is exactly the wrong move.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D068 — Cardiology · Thiazide and thiazide-like diuretics
questions.questionStem: What is the most appropriate immediate management?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 78-year-old woman admitted with pneumonia is treated with clarithromycin. Two days later, she has a witnessed syncopal episode. She is now alert. The rhythm is intermittent.

🩺 Examination:

Her blood pressure is 95/60 mmHg and her heart rate is 110 bpm.

🔬 Investigations:

An urgent ECG shows a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with QRS complexes that appear to twist around the isoelectric baseline.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
The clinical presentation and ECG findings are characteristic of Torsades de Pointes (TdP), a specific form of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia associated with a prolonged QT interval. The patient has a clear risk factor, which is the recent initiation of clarithromycin, a macrolide antibiotic known to prolong the QT interval. The management of TdP differs significantly from other forms of ventricular tachycardia.

IV magnesium sulfate is the first-line and most appropriate immediate treatment for Torsades de Pointes, regardless of the patient's baseline serum magnesium level. Magnesium is thought to stabilise the cardiac membrane and block the influx of calcium, thereby terminating the arrhythmia. It is effective in both preventing recurrent episodes and terminating ongoing ones. Given the intermittent nature of the arrhythmia described and the patient's conscious state, medical management is the priority.

  • ❌ DC cardioversion is reserved for patients with TdP who are haemodynamically unstable due to a sustained arrhythmia or who degenerate into ventricular fibrillation. In this scenario, the patient had a syncopal episode but is now conscious, and the rhythm is described as intermittent. Therefore, immediate synchronised cardioversion is not the first-line approach; medical therapy with magnesium should be administered first.
  • ❌ IV adrenaline is a key component of the cardiac arrest algorithm for pulseless ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation. This patient has a pulse and is conscious, so adrenaline is not indicated. Its administration could increase myocardial irritability and potentially provoke further arrhythmias.
  • ❌ IV amiodarone is a common treatment for many ventricular arrhythmias, but it must be used with extreme caution or avoided entirely in patients with TdP. Amiodarone itself can prolong the QT interval, and administering it could potentially worsen the arrhythmia or make it more frequent. Other antiarrhythmics that prolong the QT interval, such as sotalol and Class Ia agents, are also contraindicated.
  • ❌ Temporary cardiac pacing, specifically overdrive pacing at a rate of 90- 110 bpm, is a highly effective second-line treatment for TdP, particularly if it is recurrent or refractory to magnesium therapy. Increasing the heart rate shortens the QT interval, which suppresses the early afterdepolarisations that trigger TdP. However, it is an invasive procedure that is not the most appropriate immediate step compared to the rapid administration of intravenous magnesium.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Thiazides — the electrolyte pattern:

  • Down: sodium, potassium, magnesium
  • Up: calcium, urate (gout), glucose, lipids

They block the Na⁺/Cl⁻ cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule. Hyponatraemia is the commonest reason for stopping. A thiazide-like agent such as indapamide is the alternative when a calcium channel blocker is unsuitable because of oedema or heart failure risk.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D069 — Cardiology · Tricuspid regurgitation
questions.questionStem: What is the primary mechanism responsible for these biochemical changes?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 68-year-old man presents to the ambulatory care unit with new-onset muscle weakness. Two weeks ago, his GP initiated treatment with indapamide for hypertension. An ECG is unremarkable. His blood results are as follows: Na+ 129 mmol/L (135 - 145)

🩺 Examination:

His blood pressure is 134/82 mmHg.

🔬 Investigations:

K+ 3.2 mmol/L (3.5 - 5.0)

Urea 8.1 mmol/L (2.0 - 7.0)

Creatinine 95 µmol/L (55 - 120)

Adjusted Calcium 2.68 mmol/L (2.20 - 2.60)

#MRCP #Question

options.text: Inhibition of the Na⁺-Cl⁻ symporter in the distal convoluted tubule
Inhibition of the Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ cotransporter in the thick ascending limb
Antagonism of the aldosterone receptor in the collecting duct
Blockade of the epithelial sodium channel in the collecting duct
Inhibition of carbonic anhydrase in the proximal convoluted tubule

questions.correctAnswerText: Inhibition of the Na⁺-Cl⁻ symporter in the distal convoluted tubule
questions.explanationHtml:
Inhibition of the Na⁺-Cl⁻ symporter in the distal convoluted tubule is the correct answer. The patient has been started on indapamide, a thiazide-like diuretic. The clinical presentation of muscle weakness and the biochemical profile of hyponatraemia, hypokalaemia, and mild hypercalcaemia are characteristic adverse effects of this class of drug. Thiazide and thiazide-like diuretics exert their effect by blocking the Na⁺-Cl⁻ symporter on the apical membrane of the cells in the early distal convoluted tubule (DCT). This inhibition prevents the reabsorption of sodium and chloride, leading to natriuresis and diuresis. The increased delivery of sodium to the late DCT and collecting duct enhances its reabsorption via the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC), which in turn creates a negative electrical potential in the lumen, driving the secretion of potassium and leading to hypokalaemia. The hypercalcaemia is a key distinguishing feature; thiazides enhance calcium reabsorption in the DCT, in contrast to loop diuretics which promote calcium excretion.

  • ❌ Inhibition of the Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ cotransporter in the thick ascending limb is the mechanism of action of loop diuretics, such as furosemide and bumetanide. While these agents also cause hyponatraemia and hypokalaemia, they characteristically cause hypocalcaemia. This is because the inhibition of the Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ cotransporter disrupts the generation of the lumen-positive potential that normally drives the paracellular reabsorption of divalent cations like calcium and magnesium. The patient in this scenario has hypercalcaemia, making this mechanism incorrect.
  • ❌ Antagonism of the aldosterone receptor in the collecting duct describes the action of potassium-sparing diuretics like spironolactone and eplerenone. By blocking aldosterone's effects on the principal cells of the collecting duct, these drugs inhibit sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion. Therefore, their use is associated with hyperkalaemia, not the hypokalaemia seen in this patient. They are often used in combination with thiazide or loop diuretics to counteract the potassium-losing effects.
  • ❌ Blockade of the epithelial sodium channel in the collecting duct is the mechanism of other potassium-sparing diuretics, namely amiloride and triamterene. They directly block the ENaC channel in the principal cells of the collecting duct, independent of aldosterone. This reduces sodium reabsorption and, consequently, potassium secretion. Similar to aldosterone antagonists, their primary metabolic effect regarding potassium is hyperkalaemia, which is contrary to the patient's results.
  • ❌ Inhibition of carbonic anhydrase in the proximal convoluted tubule is the mechanism of drugs like acetazolamide. This drug inhibits the reabsorption of sodium bicarbonate from the proximal tubule, leading to a weak diuresis and a hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis. While hypokalaemia can occur, the overall biochemical picture, particularly the presence of hypercalcaemia, is not typical for a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor. This class of drug is more commonly used for glaucoma or managing altitude sickness rather than hypertension.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Giant v waves in the JVP and a pulsatile liver — tricuspid regurgitation. The pansystolic murmur is loudest at the left sternal edge and increases on inspiration.

questions.name: D070 — Cardiology · Ventricular Tachycardia – Polymorphic
questions.questionStem: What is the most likely cardiac abnormality in this case?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 40-year-old salesman presents with frequent flushing of his face and neck, abdominal pain, watery diarrhoea, fatigue, breathlessness, anorexia and nausea.

🩺 Examination:

On examination, there is jugular venous distension with prominent v waves, hepatomegaly and dependent oedema. On auscultation, a blowing pan-systolic murmur is heard on inspiration at the lower left sternal edge.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
The auscultatory findings are suggestive of tricuspid incompetence. This patient most probably has carcinoid syndrome, which can occur in 5% of patients with carcinoid tumours if there are liver metastases. Cardiac abnormalities are found in 50% of patients, and consist of pulmonary stenosis or tricuspid incompetence.

  • ❌ A. Mitral regurgitation — Mitral regurgitation is incorrect. In mitral regurgitation, a pan-systolic murmur is heard loudest at the apex and radiates widely over the precordium and into the axilla. A prominent third heart sound may be present. Mitral regurgitation does not usually occur due to carcinoid syndrome.
  • ❌ C. Tricuspid stenosis — Tricuspid stenosis is incorrect. A rumbling mid-diastolic murmur is characteristic of tricuspid stenosis along with a prominent jugular venous a wave.
  • ❌ D. Pulmonary stenosis — Pulmonary stenosis is incorrect. In pulmonary stenosis, the characteristic auscultatory finding is a harsh mid- systolic ejection murmur best heard on inspiration to the left of the sternum in the second intercostal space. A right ventricular fourth sound and a prominent jugular venous a wave is present if the stenosis is moderately severe.
  • ❌ E. Prolapsing mitral valve — Prolapsing mitral valve is incorrect. A prolapsing ('floppy') mitral valve is commonly seen in young women and has a familial incidence. It may be associated with rheumatic or ischaemic heart disease, Marfan syndrome or thyrotoxicosis. The most common sign is a mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur due to some regurgitation. Further reading: [patient.info/doctor/carcinoid-tumours](http://patient.info/doctor/carcinoid-tumours) ([http://patient.info/doctor/carcinoid-tumours)

#MRCP](http://patient.info/doctor/carcinoid-tumours)

#MRCP) #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Polymorphic VT with a long baseline QT is torsades de pointes; with a normal QT it usually means acute ischaemia. The distinction changes the treatment entirely.

questions.name: D071 — Cardiology · Ventricular septal defect
questions.questionStem: Which one of the following would be your initial line of treatment?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 68-year-old man is admitted with syncope. He is known to have ischaemic cardiomyopathy. His medications are aspirin (75 mg, once daily), furosemide (80 mg, twice daily) and lisinopril (10 mg, once daily). He has recurrent syncopal episodes on the coronary care unit, where monitoring shows episodes of non-sustained torsades de pointes (polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (VT)).

🔬 Investigations:

An initial electrocardiogram (ECG) shows sinus bradycardia (50 bpm) and right branch bundle block. Results of blood tests are: sodium, 134 mmol/l; potassium, 3.5 mmol/l; creatinine, 124 µmol/l.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
Torsades de pointes (polymorphic VT with QRS complexes of different amplitude twisting around the isoelectric line) occurs in patients with a prolonged QT interval. Any cause of QT prolongation can predispose to the arrhythmia. Causes include congenital (Jervell–Lange-Nielsen or Romano–Ward syndromes), QRS complexes of different amplitude, metabolic (hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia or hypokalaemia), drugs (e.g. amiodarone, tricyclic antidepressants, phenothiazines), ischaemic heart disease and mitral valve prolapse. The arrhythmia often occurs in the context of bradycardia. Intravenous magnesium (even if the serum concentration of magnesium is normal) is first-line therapy.

External Links

Torsades de Pointes [patient.info/doctor/torsades-de-pointes](http://patient.info/doctor/torsades-de-pointes) ([https://patient.info/doctor/torsades-de-pointes)

  • ❌](https://patient.info/doctor/torsades-de-pointes)

    • ❌) A. DC cardioversion — DC cardioversion is incorrect. DC shock would not be helpful because episodes are non-sustained.
    • ❌ B. Intravenous amiodarone — Intravenous amiodarone is incorrect. Amiodarone prolongs the action potential, it doesn’t actually cause torsades, but it doesn’t drive any benefit for patients.
    • ❌ D. Oral metoprolol — Oral metoprolol is incorrect. Temporary pacing at higher rates, with or without beta blockers, would be the next line of therapy, but the initial treatment would be intravenous magnesium.
    • ❌ E. Temporary pacing — Temporary pacing is incorrect. As stated above, initial management is intravenous magnesium.

questions.pearlHtml:
💡

The smaller the ventricular septal defect, the louder the murmur — a harsh pansystolic murmur at the left sternal edge with a thrill often signals a haemodynamically trivial lesion.
