questions.name: D072 — Cardiology · Warfarin
questions.questionStem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 21-year-old man with Down syndrome presents to the Emergency Department with worsening shortness of breath. He tells you this has increased significantly over the last few months and he is now unable to go out with his friends.

🩺 Examination:

On examination, he is clubbed and cyanosed at rest, his BP is 145/82 mmHg and pulse is 85/min. The patient has previously been noted to have a harsh systolic murmur at the left sternal edge which is now less audible.

🔬 Investigations:

Routine chest X-ray carried out by his GP a few weeks earlier shows prominent pulmonary vasculature, but nil else of note.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
Atrioventricular septal defects (AVSDs) are the commonest cardiovascular abnormality seen in Down syndrome; the next most commonly seen are VSDs and ASDs. In this case the murmur is typical of that seen in VSD, and the clinical picture raises the possibility of a significant right to left shunt. Two-dimensional echocardiography coupled with Doppler flow analysis can be used to quantify the location of the lesion and estimate the size of any shunt. This patient should have a surgical consultation to determine surgical repair is indicated, although late presentation with evidence of shunt is associated with a poor outlook. Smaller VSDs may spontaneously close during childhood.

  • ❌ A. Aortic stenosis — Aortic stenosis is incorrect. Aortic stenosis is more common in elderly patients with atherosclerotic heart disease. It would present with an ejection systolic murmur.
  • ❌ B. Atrial septal defect — Atrial septal defect is incorrect. Atrial septal defect occurs when there is absence of the septum that divides the left and right atria, as a result of a congenital defect. The signs include a systolic ejection murmur due to the pulmonic valve. In unaffected individuals, respiratory variations occur in the splitting of the second heart sound. A fixed splitting of S2 may occur.
  • ❌ C. Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy — Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy is incorrect. Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy is a hypertrophied myocardium without an obvious cause, creating functional impairment. It is the leading cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes. There may be an ejection systolic murmur.
  • ❌ D. Patent ductus arteriosus — Patent ductus arteriosus is incorrect. This is a condition where the ductus arteriosus fails to close after birth. An uncorrected patent ductus arteriosus may lead to congestive cardiac failure with increasing age. Symptoms include tachycardia, dyspnoea and a continuous ‘machine-like’ heart murmur (usually from aorta to pulmonary artery, with higher flow during systole and lower flow during diastole). There may be cardiomegaly, left subclavicular thrill, bounding pulse, widened pulse pressure and increased systolic pressure with high cardiac output.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, depleting factors II, VII, IX and X plus proteins C and S.

  • Protein C has the shortest half-life, so there is a transient procoagulant window at initiation — hence warfarin-induced skin necrosis
  • Factor VII has the shortest half-life of the procoagulant factors and drives the early INR rise
  • Enzyme inducers (rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St John's wort) lower the INR; inhibitors (macrolides, azoles, ciprofloxacin, cranberry juice) raise it

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D073 — Cardiology · Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome
questions.questionStem: Which one of the following is most likely to be responsible?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 63-year-old female on long-term warfarin for atrial fibrillation attends the anticoagulation clinic. Despite having a stable INR for the past 4 years on the same dose of warfarin her INR is measured at 5.4.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
The correct answer is cranberry juice. Cranberry juice has been shown to potentiate the anticoagulant effect of warfarin by inhibiting the cytochrome P450 2C9 (CYP2C9) enzyme system, which is responsible for metabolising warfarin. This interaction can lead to a significant increase in INR values and potentially dangerous bleeding complications. The effect can occur within days of starting regular cranberry juice consumption.

  • ❌ St John's Wort actually has the opposite effect on warfarin metabolism. It induces the CYP2C9 enzyme system, leading to increased warfarin metabolism and consequently reduced anticoagulant effect and lower INR values. This would not explain the elevated INR in this case.
  • ❌ Smoking also induces hepatic enzymes and typically reduces the anticoagulant effect of warfarin, requiring higher doses to maintain therapeutic INR. If a patient stops smoking, their warfarin requirements may decrease, but ongoing smoking would not cause an elevated INR.
  • ❌ Carrot juice contains vitamin K which would antagonise the effect of warfarin by promoting coagulation factor synthesis. This would lead to a reduced INR rather than the elevation seen in this case.
  • ❌ Camomile tea, while it contains natural coumarin compounds, has not been consistently shown to have a clinically significant interaction with warfarin when consumed in normal quantities as a beverage. Any theoretical interaction would be unlikely to cause such a marked elevation in INR.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Wolff-Parkinson-White: short PR, delta wave, broad QRS from ventricular pre-excitation via an accessory pathway.

  • Pre-excited atrial fibrillation is the dangerous presentation — irregular, broad, very fast
  • Avoid AV nodal blocking drugs (adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin, beta-blockers): blocking the node drives conduction down the accessory pathway and can precipitate ventricular fibrillation
  • Definitive treatment is accessory pathway ablation

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D074 — Cardiology · Cardiomyopathy
questions.questionStem: What is the most appropriate pharmacological management option for this patient?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

You are a CT1 in Acute Medicine covering the hospital at night. You are called to the surgical ward to see a 35-year-old patient who is reporting palpitations. She is known to have Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.

🩺 Examination:

On examination, there is no evidence of haemodynamic instability.

🔬 Investigations:

Her ECG shows fast atrial fibrillation.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
In patients with accessory pathways, such as those with Wolff-Parkinson- White syndrome, AV nodal blocking drugs should be avoided in atrial fibrillation. This is because blocking the AV node may enhance the rate of conduction through the accessory pathway, causing atrial fibrillation to degenerate into ventricular fibrillation (VF).

Verapamil exerts the most reliable and long-lasting effect on AV node refractoriness and therefore is the most contra-indicated in this scenario. Adenosine has a similar effect and has also been associated with precipitating VF in pre-excited atrial fibrillation.

Beta-blockers and digoxin also inhibit AV node conduction.

Flecainide is a sodium channel blocker (Class Ic anti-arrhythmic) which will reduce the excitability of the atrial and ventricular myocardium without AV nodal blockade.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Takotsubo cardiomyopathy: apical ballooning with ST elevation and raised troponin after intense emotional or physical stress, but unobstructed coronary arteries and recovery over weeks.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D075 — Cardiology · ECG interpretation
questions.questionStem: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 34-year-old professional footballer is evaluated for symptoms of ‘dizziness’ during exercise.

🩺 Examination:

Physical examination reveals a laterally displaced apical impulse. On auscultation, there is a 2/6 mid-systolic murmur in the aortic area that increases on sudden standing.

🔬 Investigations:

The ECG shows LVH and Q waves in the V2–V5 leads.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
In this case, we should consider the causes of a mid-systolic murmur in the aortic area in a young patient. This is the correct answer because the features are all consistent with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Patients classically have a systolic murmur that becomes worse on standing and becomes quieter on squatting. Patients typically complain of dizziness on exertion and have displaced and forceful apex. ECGs in HCM typically have LVH. Other ECG changes can give the appearances of ischaemia despite normal coronary arteries; deep T-wave inversion or anterior Q waves are common.

Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy

Adverse effects:

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the single most common cause of sudden death in young athletes Syncope and sudden death are associated with severe exertion and competitive sports, which should be avoided in patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

Symptoms:

The majority of patients are asymptomatic or only mildly symptomatic The most common symptom is dyspnea.

Examination and investigation findings

Typical examination findings include: left ventricular hypertrophy a loud S4 forceful atrial systole causing a double apical impulse a possible triple apical impulse due to a late systolic bulge the carotid pulse demonstrates a late systolic pulse causing the characteristic jerky feature.

In contrast to aortic stenosis, the systolic murmur of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: does not radiate to the carotids decreases on squatting and passive leg elevation and increases with the Valsalva manoeuvre.

ECG:

The most common changes seen on the ECG are ST–T wave abnormalities followed by left ventricular hypertrophy Q waves may also occur in leads II, III, aVF or V2–V6 The exact cause of the Q waves remains unclear.

  • ❌ A. Young-onset hypertension — Young onset hypertension is incorrect. The given findings do not support this as the most likely diagnosis.
  • ❌ B. Acute MI — Acute MI is incorrect. Acute MI is unlikely because the patient is young and has not complained of chest pain.
  • ❌ C. Aortic stenosis — Aortic stenosis is incorrect. Aortic stenosis causes an ejection systolic murmur and is unlikely in a 34-year-old patient; it typically manifests in the 60–70s. Even patients with a bicuspid valve related aortic stenosis are in their 50s.
  • ❌ E. Atrial septal defect — Atrial septal defect is incorrect. Atrial septal defects are typically associated with right bundle branch block. Patients have a fixed split second heart sound. If the shunt is significant, there may be a mid-diastolic flow murmur over the tricuspid area.

questions.pearlHtml:

Left bundle branch block is never a normal variant — it always implies underlying structural or conduction disease, and it renders the ST segments uninterpretable for ischaemia.

questions.name: D076 — Cardiology · Heart Sounds
questions.questionStem: Each one of the following may cause left bundle branch block, except:
questions.explanationHtml:
The correct answer is Atrial septal defect (ostium secundum). Atrial septal defect (ASD) of the ostium secundum type does not typically cause left bundle branch block (LBBB). An ostium secundum ASD is a congenital heart defect characterised by a defect in the interatrial septum allowing blood flow between the left and right atria. While ASDs can lead to various cardiac complications such as right heart volume overload, right ventricular hypertrophy, and atrial arrhythmias, they do not typically affect the left bundle branch of the cardiac conduction system. The left bundle branch is anatomically distant from the atrial septum, and the pathophysiological changes associated with an ASD primarily affect the right side of the heart rather than the left ventricular conduction system.

  • ❌ Cardiomyopathy is an incorrect option as it can cause LBBB. Cardiomyopathies, particularly dilated cardiomyopathy, involve myocardial damage and fibrosis that can disrupt the cardiac conduction system. The left bundle branch is particularly vulnerable in cardiomyopathies due to its anatomical location and the diffuse myocardial involvement characteristic of these conditions. Progressive fibrosis and myocardial remodelling in cardiomyopathy can directly damage the left bundle branch, leading to LBBB.
  • ❌ Hypertension is an incorrect option as it is a well-established cause of LBBB. Chronic hypertension leads to left ventricular hypertrophy and increased myocardial wall stress. Over time, this can result in myocardial fibrosis and disruption of the cardiac conduction system, particularly affecting the left bundle branch. The mechanical strain and subsequent structural remodelling in hypertensive heart disease create an environment conducive to conduction abnormalities, including LBBB.
  • ❌ Idiopathic fibrosis is an incorrect option as it can cause LBBB. Idiopathic fibrosis of the cardiac conduction system, also known as Lev's disease or Lenègre's disease, directly affects the bundle branches. This progressive degenerative process involves fibrosis and sclerosis of the conduction system, often with a predilection for the left bundle branch due to its longer and more complex anatomical structure. The fibrotic changes disrupt electrical impulse propagation, resulting in LBBB.
  • ❌ Ischaemic heart disease is an incorrect option as it is a common cause of LBBB. Coronary artery disease can lead to myocardial ischaemia and infarction, particularly affecting the left anterior descending artery which supplies the interventricular septum where the left bundle branch is located. Acute ischaemia can cause transient LBBB, while myocardial infarction can result in permanent LBBB due to necrosis and subsequent fibrosis of the conduction tissue. Chronic ischaemia can also lead to progressive fibrosis and disruption of the left bundle branch.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Splitting of the second heart sound: fixed in atrial septal defect, wide in right bundle branch block and pulmonary stenosis, reversed (paradoxical) in left bundle branch block, aortic stenosis and right ventricular pacing.

questions.name: D077 — Cardiology · Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy
questions.questionStem: Given the ECG findings, which one of the following is most likely to be found on auscultation of the heart?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 71-year-old man with a history of ischaemic heart disease is brought to the Emergency Department following a 'collapse'. He now feels back to normal.

🔬 Investigations:

The ECG shows sinus rhythm, 94/min with left bundle branch block.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
The correct answer is Reversed split S2. In left bundle branch block (LBBB), there is a delay in the electrical activation of the left ventricle compared to the right ventricle. This delay affects the timing of ventricular contraction and subsequently the closure of the heart valves. The second heart sound (S2) consists of two components: aortic valve closure (A2) and pulmonary valve closure (P2). Normally, A2 precedes P2. However, in LBBB, the delayed left ventricular contraction leads to delayed aortic valve closure. This causes A2 to occur after P2, resulting in a reversed splitting of S2. Importantly, this reversed splitting is heard during expiration (unlike normal physiological splitting which is heard during inspiration) and persists throughout the respiratory cycle, making it a characteristic finding in patients with LBBB.

  • ❌ Fixed split S2 is incorrect in this context. A fixed split S2 is typically associated with atrial septal defects (ASD), where the splitting of S2 remains constant throughout the respiratory cycle due to the persistent right ventricular volume overload. In LBBB, we would expect a reversed split S2 rather than a fixed split.
  • ❌ Loud S1 is incorrect. The first heart sound (S1) is produced by the closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves. In LBBB, there is no specific mechanism that would lead to a consistently louder S1. In fact, S1 might be normal or even diminished in intensity due to the asynchronous ventricular contraction.
  • ❌ Third heart sound (S3) is incorrect for this patient's presentation. An S3 is a low-pitched sound heard in early diastole, often associated with heart failure and volume overload conditions. While this patient has a history of ischaemic heart disease, there is no indication of heart failure in the scenario. LBBB itself does not typically cause an S3 gallop, although it's worth noting that patients with LBBB often have underlying structural heart disease which might lead to an S3 in some cases.
  • ❌ Widely split S2 is incorrect. A widely split S2 occurs when there is a delay in right ventricular emptying, causing P2 to be delayed relative to A2. This is commonly seen in right bundle branch block (RBBB), not LBBB. In LBBB, the left ventricular emptying is delayed, leading to a reversed split S2 where A2 follows P2, which is the opposite of a widely split S2.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy:

  • Autosomal dominant mutations in sarcomere genes — most often MYH7 (beta-myosin heavy chain) and MYBPC3 (myosin-binding protein C)
  • Outflow obstruction arises from systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve, which also produces mitral regurgitation
  • ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy with deep T-wave inversion; apical disease gives giant precordial T-wave inversion
  • It is the commonest cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes

questions.name: D078 — Cardiology · Long QT syndrome
questions.questionStem: What is the most likely genetic mutation responsible for his condition?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 22-year-old male presents to the cardiology clinic with exertional dyspnoea and two episodes of syncope while playing football. His father died suddenly at age 40.

🩺 Examination:

On examination, he has a jerky pulse and a systolic murmur that increases with Valsalva manoeuvre.

🔬 Investigations:

Echocardiogram shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy and systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
Myosin-binding protein C gene is the correct answer. This patient presents with classic features of hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM), including exertional dyspnoea, exercise- induced syncope, family history of sudden cardiac death, and characteristic examination findings (jerky pulse and systolic murmur that increases with Valsalva). The echocardiogram confirms the diagnosis with asymmetric septal hypertrophy and systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve. HOCM is most commonly caused by mutations in genes encoding sarcomeric proteins, with myosin-binding protein C (MYBPC3) and β- myosin heavy chain (MYH7) accounting for approximately 70-80% of genotyped cases. MYBPC3 mutations are the most common, found in about 40-50% of genotype-positive patients. These mutations lead to disorganized myocardial architecture and fibrosis, resulting in the pathophysiological features of HOCM.

  • ❌ Dystrophin gene mutations are responsible for Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophies. While these conditions can have cardiac involvement (typically dilated cardiomyopathy), they primarily present with skeletal muscle weakness and elevated creatine kinase levels. The patient's presentation with isolated cardiac symptoms without skeletal muscle involvement makes dystrophin gene mutations unlikely.
  • ❌ Lamin A/C gene mutations cause laminopathies, including Emery- Dreifuss muscular dystrophy and familial dilated cardiomyopathy with conduction defects. These typically present with early conduction abnormalities, atrial arrhythmias, and dilated cardiomyopathy rather than hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. The echocardiographic findings in this case are inconsistent with laminopathies.
  • ❌ Troponin T gene mutations can cause HOCM, but they account for only about 5% of genotyped cases, making them less likely than myosin- binding protein C mutations. Troponin T mutations are associated with milder hypertrophy but a higher risk of sudden cardiac death. While this could fit with the family history, the prevalence makes it less likely than MYBPC3.
  • ❌ Titin gene mutations are primarily associated with dilated cardiomyopathy and some cases of arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy. They are not typically associated with HOCM. The echocardiographic findings of asymmetric septal hypertrophy and systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve are inconsistent with titin gene mutations.

Drugs that lengthen the QT cluster into a few families: antiarrhythmics (amiodarone, sotalol), macrolides and quinolones, antipsychotics, tricyclics and citalopram, antifungals, ondansetron, and methadone. Hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and hypocalcaemia compound them all.

questions.name: D079 — Cardiology · Pacemakers
questions.questionStem: Given the electrolyte abnormality she is likely to have developed, what ECG abnormality is most associated with this?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

An 84-year-old female with a background of osteoporosis is given an infusion of pamidronate. A week later she presents to her GP complaining of paraesthesia.

🩺 Examination:

On examination she has hyperreflexia and carpopedal spasm.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
Long QT is associated with hypocalcaemia. Bisphosphonate infusions can lead to hypocalcaemia although it is more common when using larger doses in malignancy induced hypercalcaemia as oppose to the smaller dose used in osteoporosis.

A QT interval of greater than 0.44 seconds is associated with the development of ventricular arrhythmia, syncope and sudden cardiac death.

Long QT causes: electrolyte abnormalities: hypokalemia and hypocalcemia drugs: tricyclic antidepressants, antihistamines, erythromycin, clarithromycin, amiodarone, haloperidol congenital long QT syndromes: more than 10 different types recognised myocardial infarction/significant active myocardial ischemia cerebrovascular accident (subarachnoid haemorrhage)

hypothermia

Hyperreflexia and carpopedal spasm indicate neuromuscular irritability which is a feature of hypocalcaemia. Chvostek's sign can also be elicited by tapping over the facial nerve at the angle of the jaw. A positive result would involve ipsilateral twitching of the muscles around the nose and lips.

questions.questionStem: Which of the following is the best treatment option?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 17-year-old man had a cardiac arrest while playing football and was resuscitated. He recovered fully and was later found to have hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM).

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
For secondary prevention of sudden cardiac death (SCD) in patients with HOCM, there is evidence and general agreement that an ICD is the most useful option.

  • ❌ B. Amiodarone — Amiodarone is incorrect. That said, in the primary prevention of SCD in HOCM, amiodarone may have a role in some patients. However, the general consensus is that primary prevention via an ICD is the preferred option.
  • ❌ C. Beta Blockers — Beta blockers is incorrect. Beta blockers aid HOCM management because they can slow down the heart rate and reduce the likelihood of ectopic beats. However, this strategy should be followed after the patient has been treated correctly with an ICD in the acute setting.
  • ❌ D. Verapamil — Verapamil is incorrect. Verapamil aids HOCM management because it can slow down the heart rate and reduce the likelihood of ectopic beats. That said, for patients who cannot tolerate beta blockers or do not have good control of symptoms with beta blockers, non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers such as verapamil can be used. However, non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers are potentially harmful in patients in a setting of systemic hypotension or severe dyspnoea at rest. These medications also reduce the heart rate, though their use in patients with severe outflow obstruction, elevated pulmonary artery wedge pressure, and low blood pressures should be followed with expert guidance.
  • ❌ E. Rate-responsive, dual-chamber pacemaker — Rate-responsive, dual-chamber pacemaker is incorrect. Biventricular pacing will not help reduce the risk of cardiac arrest and will not have a useful impact in cardiac arrest because this type of device does not have a defibrillator function. 889

questions.name: D082 — Cardiology · Pulmonary arterial hypertension
questions.questionStem: What would be the treatment of choice?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

An echocardiogram confirms severe valvular disease. The cardiology consultant decides that valve replacement is required.

🩺 Examination:

A 22-year-old man presents with worsening peripheral oedema and shortness of breath. On examination, you note a pansystolic murmur and soft S1.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
Mechanical mitral valve is correct. The auscultatory findings are highly suggestive of mitral regurgitation. The cause for this should also be established, and in a patient of this age, cardiomyopathy, endocarditis and rheumatic fever would be high up the differential diagnosis list. In general, younger patients should be provided with a mechanical heart valve since these have a significantly greater lifespan compared to bioprosthetic valves. The average lifespan of a bioprosthetic valve is estimated to be approximately 15 years. However, the major disadvantage of mechanical heart valves is the fact they need lifelong anticoagulation with warfarin. Therefore for some patients (e.g. females of childbearing potential, and those with substantial bleeding risk factors), a bioprosthetic valve is the best choice.

  • ❌ Mechanical aortic valve is incorrect. The clinical features suggest mitral regurgitation. Aortic stenosis would present with an ejection systolic murmur, whilst aortic regurgitation would present with an early diastolic murmur.
  • ❌ Mechanical pulmonary valve is incorrect. The clinical features suggest mitral regurgitation. Pulmonary stenosis would present with an ejection systolic murmur, whilst pulmonary regurgitation would present with an early diastolic murmur.
  • ❌ Prosthetic aortic valve is incorrect. The clinical features suggest mitral regurgitation. Aortic stenosis would present with an ejection systolic murmur, whilst aortic regurgitation would present with an early diastolic murmur.
  • ❌ Prosthetic mitral valve is incorrect. The clinical features suggest mitral regurgitation. As discussed above, given the patient's age, and the limited life span of a bioprosthetic valve, a mechanical valve is usually preferred in this cohort of patients.

questions.name: D083 — Cardiology · Pulmonary embolism
questions.questionStem: What would be the single best initial treatment?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 56-year-old woman presents with progressive shortness of breath and fatigue over the past few months. She has no chest pain and no significant past medical history. The pulmonary component of the second heart sound is accentuated. Given the suspected diagnosis, vasodilator testing is arranged, to which the patient has a negative response.

🩺 Examination:

On examination, the chest is clear.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
The diagnosis here is pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), given the symptoms of progressive breathlessness and fatigue and the heart sound findings. Vasodilator testing is used to identify the small subset of patients who respond to oral calcium-channel blockers. The vast majority of patients have a negative response to vasodilator testing, as in the scenario above. These patients should be treated with prostacyclin analogues, endothelin receptor antagonists or phosphodiesterase inhibitors. The only suitable medication in this scenario is sildenafil, a phosphodiesterase inhibitor.

  • ❌ Digoxin is occasionally used as an adjunct in a select group of patients with PAH - those with refractory right heart failure or supraventricular arrhythmias. It is not routinely used, and in the scenario above, sildenafil remains the best choice initially.
  • ❌ Diltiazem is a rate-limiting calcium channel blocker and may have been used if the patient had a positive response to vasodilator testing. A rate- limiting blocker would be more suitable in patients with higher baseline heart rates.
  • ❌ Furosemide is a loop diuretic and is sometimes used as an adjunct to relieve fluid retention associated with right heart failure. It is not directly a first-line treatment option for PAH.
  • ❌ Nifedipine is a non-rate-limiting calcium channel blocker and would be used if the patient had a positive response to vasodilator testing. In the scenario above, as testing was negative, sildenafil is most appropriate.

Two-level Wells score directs the pathway:

  • PE likely (>4 points) → immediate CTPA; if delayed, give interim anticoagulation
  • PE unlikely (≤4 points) → D-dimer; if positive, proceed to CTPA; if negative, PE is excluded

V/Q scanning replaces CTPA where there is renal impairment, contrast allergy, or pregnancy.

questions.name: D084 — Cardiology · Acute coronary syndrome
questions.questionStem: What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 28-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a two- day history of sharp, left-sided chest pain, worse on deep inspiration and movement. He has no past medical history. There is no unilateral leg swelling.

🩺 Examination:

The pain is reproducible on palpation of the third intercostal space. His observations are: heart rate 84 bpm, respiratory rate 16/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.

#MRCP #Question

options.text: Discharge with no further investigation for PE
Admit for observation and serial troponins

questions.correctAnswerText: Discharge with no further investigation for PE
questions.explanationHtml:
Discharge with no further investigation for PE is the correct answer. According to NICE guideline NG158, the first step in assessing a patient with suspected pulmonary embolism (PE) is to estimate the clinical probability. This patient has a very low pre-test probability of PE. A clear alternative diagnosis of musculoskeletal chest pain is present, supported by the pain being reproducible on palpation. In such cases, where the clinician's overall impression is that PE is unlikely and other diagnoses are feasible, the Pulmonary Embolism Rule-out Criteria (PERC) should be applied. The eight PERC criteria are: age <50, heart rate <100 bpm, oxygen saturation >94%, no unilateral leg swelling, no haemoptysis, no recent surgery/trauma, no prior DVT/PE, and no oestrogen use. This patient meets all the criteria for a negative PERC score (i.e., all criteria are absent). A negative PERC score reduces the probability of PE to less than 2%, meaning PE can be safely excluded without further investigations like a D-dimer or imaging. The patient can be discharged with advice regarding their likely musculoskeletal pain.

  • ❌ Arrange a D-dimer test is incorrect. A D-dimer test is the appropriate next step for patients with a low clinical probability of PE (Wells score ≤4) after the PERC rule has been considered and is not applicable (i.e., one or more PERC criteria are present). The purpose of the PERC rule is to identify a cohort of very low-risk patients who do not even require a D- dimer, thereby avoiding the high rate of false-positive D-dimer results which can lead to unnecessary imaging, radiation exposure, and patient anxiety. As this patient is PERC-negative, proceeding to a D-dimer is not indicated and represents an unnecessary investigation.
  • ❌ Arrange a CT pulmonary angiogram is incorrect. A CT pulmonary angiogram (CTPA) is the definitive imaging for diagnosing PE. It is indicated for patients where PE is considered 'likely' (Wells score >4), or in patients where PE is 'unlikely' (Wells score ≤4) but they have a positive D-dimer result. This patient has a Wells score of 0, and as he is PERC- negative, no further investigation is warranted. Proceeding directly to a CTPA in such a low-risk patient would expose them to significant unnecessary radiation and intravenous contrast with no clinical justification.
  • ❌ Arrange a ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) scan is also incorrect. A V/Q scan is an alternative imaging modality to CTPA for diagnosing PE. It is generally considered in patients who have a contraindication to CTPA, such as severe renal impairment or a history of anaphylaxis to contrast media. It is not a first-line investigation in this patient and, more importantly, no imaging is required at all as PE has been effectively ruled out on clinical grounds using the PERC rule. The diagnostic pathway should not proceed to imaging in this scenario.
  • ❌ Admit for observation and serial troponins is not the most appropriate step. While an acute coronary syndrome (ACS) is a differential for chest pain, this patient's presentation makes it highly unlikely. His age is low, and the pain has clear musculoskeletal features (sharp, localised, reproducible on palpation). While a single baseline troponin may be checked in the Emergency Department as part of a chest pain workup, admission for serial troponins is not indicated given the low pre-test probability for ACS. The question focuses on the management pathway for suspected PE, which has been ruled out.

Secondary prevention after myocardial infarction — four drug classes, offered to everyone:

  • ACE inhibitor, continued indefinitely
  • Dual antiplatelet therapy (unless there is a separate anticoagulation indication)
  • Beta-blocker
  • Statin

Add an aldosterone antagonist within 3 to 14 days for those with heart failure and reduced ejection fraction, preferably after the ACE inhibitor is established.

questions.name: D085 — Cardiology · Aortic stenosis
questions.questionStem: Four weeks following the event, which combination of drugs should he be taking?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 58-year-old man with no past medical history of note is admitted to hospital with crushing central chest pain. ECG on arrival shows anterior ST elevation and he is subsequently thrombolysed with a good resolution of symptoms and ECG changes.

#MRCP #Question

options.text: ACE inhibitor + beta-blocker + statin + aspirin + ticagrelor

questions.correctAnswerText: ACE inhibitor + beta-blocker + statin + aspirin + ticagrelor
questions.explanationHtml:
The correct answer is ACE inhibitor + beta-blocker + statin + aspirin + ticagrelor. Following an ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), current guidelines recommend dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) with aspirin plus a P2Y12 inhibitor (preferably ticagrelor) for 12 months. Additionally, patients should receive an ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker and high-intensity statin for secondary prevention.

  • ❌ ACE inhibitor + beta-blocker + statin + aspirin is incorrect as it only includes single antiplatelet therapy. Following STEMI, DAPT is essential to prevent stent thrombosis and reduce recurrent cardiovascular events.
  • ❌ Spironolactone + beta-blocker + statin + aspirin is incorrect. While spironolactone has a role in heart failure management, it is not routinely indicated post-MI unless there is significant left ventricular dysfunction (ejection fraction ≤40%) or heart failure.
  • ❌ ACE inhibitor + statin + aspirin + clopidogrel is incorrect as it omits a beta-blocker, which is essential post-MI to reduce mortality and prevent arrhythmias. While clopidogrel is an acceptable P2Y12 inhibitor, ticagrelor is preferred due to superior outcomes.
  • ❌ Beta-blocker + statin + aspirin + clopidogrel is incorrect as it omits an ACE inhibitor, which is important for reducing adverse cardiac remodelling post-MI and improving long-term outcomes.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Exertional syncope with a systolic murmur demands urgent assessment — it carries a high risk of poor outcome, and severe aortic stenosis found this way usually needs intervention.

questions.name: D086 — Cardiology · Ventricular tachycardia
questions.questionStem: What is the most appropriate management?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 72-year-old man is referred to cardiology clinic with exertional dyspnoea. His left ventricular ejection fraction is 55%. He has no other significant comorbidities.

🩺 Examination:

He has a harsh ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids.

🔬 Investigations:

An echocardiogram shows a calcified aortic valve with a peak gradient of 45 mmHg and a valve area of 0.9 cm².

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
Aortic valve replacement is the correct management for this patient. He has symptomatic severe aortic stenosis, evidenced by his exertional dyspnoea, a peak gradient of 45 mmHg (>40 mmHg indicates severe stenosis), and a valve area of 0.9 cm² (<1.0 cm² defines severe stenosis). The presence of symptoms in aortic stenosis is a critical decision point for intervention, regardless of stenosis severity. However, this patient has both symptoms and severe stenosis, making the indication for valve replacement clear. Symptomatic severe aortic stenosis carries a poor prognosis without intervention, with survival rates of approximately 50% at 2 years. Given his age and lack of significant comorbidities, he would likely be considered for either surgical AVR or transcatheter AVR (TAVR), with the specific approach determined after further risk assessment.

  • ❌ Annual echocardiographic surveillance would be appropriate for asymptomatic patients with mild to moderate aortic stenosis. This patient has both symptoms and severe stenosis, making surveillance alone inappropriate and potentially dangerous. Without intervention, his symptoms will likely progress, and he faces significant risk of sudden cardiac death, heart failure, and other complications.
  • ❌ Balloon aortic valvuloplasty is not recommended as definitive therapy for adults with calcific aortic stenosis. It provides only temporary relief of stenosis, with high restenosis rates within 6-12 months. It may be considered as a bridge to definitive valve replacement in critically ill patients or in rare cases where valve replacement is contraindicated. In this relatively healthy 72-year-old, it would not be the most appropriate management option.
  • ❌ Medical therapy with beta-blockers is not indicated for the management of aortic stenosis itself. Beta-blockers may actually be harmful in isolated aortic stenosis as they can reduce cardiac output and exacerbate symptoms. While medical therapy may help manage symptoms in patients who are not candidates for valve replacement, it does not alter the natural history of the disease or improve survival in symptomatic severe aortic stenosis.
  • ❌ Reassurance and discharge would be inappropriate for a patient with symptomatic severe aortic stenosis. Without intervention, symptomatic aortic stenosis has a poor prognosis with mortality rates of approximately 25% at 1 year and 50% at 2 years. The presence of symptoms indicates that the disease has reached a critical stage requiring definitive intervention.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Pulseless ventricular tachycardia is a shockable rhythm — treated identically to ventricular fibrillation. With a pulse and adverse features, it is synchronised cardioversion instead.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D087 — Cardiology · Angina pectoris
questions.questionStem: Which drug, if given, is most likely to precipitate severe hypotension, ventricular fibrillation or cardiac arrest in this patient and should therefore be avoided?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 28-year-old man who is normally fit and well presents with palpitations. He has no chest pain. An electrocardiogram (ECG) is completed: Rate 170 beats/min, regular, QRS 140ms with uniform appearance, right ECG bundle branch pattern. There is no previous ECG to compare to.

🩺 Examination:

Apart from tachycardia his examination is unremarkable. His blood pressure is 105/70mmHg and his heart rate is 170 beats/min and regular.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
The answer is verapamil.

In broad complex tachycardia with adverse features (shock with SBP <90, syncope, ischaemia/chest pain, heart failure), synchronised DC cardioversion should be performed. If there are no adverse features, pharmacological options can be considered.

Some patients (particularly younger patients with no history of heart disease) may have a broad complex tachycardia due to supraventricular tachycardia with aberrant conduction. However, clinical features alone do not rule out VT and a broad complex tachycardia should generally be assumed to be ventricular in origin.

Although not advised by Resuscitation Council guidelines, adenosine is felt to be safe to give in broad complex tachycardia and some guidelines advise it can help diagnosis if it corrects the rhythm, although this is controversial as some ventricular tachycardias will respond to adenosine. (Adenosine should however definitely be avoided in irregular broad complex tachycardia as it can precipitate ventricular fibrillation).

Amiodarone, lidocaine and procainamide are all potential therapeutic options for ventricular tachycardia in this patient without structural heart disease.

Verapamil is an option for termination of supraventricular tachycardia (SVT). However, it should be avoided here as we do not know for certain whether this is SVT or VT. If it is VT, verapamil may precipitate cardiac arrest.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

When combining a calcium channel blocker with a beta-blocker in angina, it must be a dihydropyridine — amlodipine or a modified-release nifedipine, never verapamil or diltiazem.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D088 — Cardiology · Atrial fibrillation
questions.questionStem: What alteration should be made to this patient's management?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

The pain is exercise dependent with it occurring when the patient carries out activities such as climbing stairs and resolving on rest. As such the patient was started on atenolol 100mg OD along with a GTN spray and aspirin. On review today the patient still reports symptoms of chest pain on exertion despite good compliance.

🔬 Investigations:

A 52-year-old man is seen in the clinic after originally being referred with progressively increasing central chest pain but base level investigations, including ECGs and troponin level return within normal range.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
This patient is suffering from symptoms in keeping with angina and has been correctly commenced on a beta-blocker along with aspirin and GTN spray as first-line therapy. As the patient is still experiencing symptoms, despite being on the maximum dose of a beta-blocker, a calcium channel blocker should be added. When used in combination with a beta-blocker a longer-acting dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker e.g. modified-release nifedipine should be used to improve symptom control whilst avoiding the risk of heart block dysrhythmias. A long-acting/modified-release version of the medication should ideally be used.

Diltiazem may be commenced as monotherapy initially for patients presenting with angina however its use with beta-blockers should be avoided as this can lead to significant adverse effects on cardiac conduction, heart rate and contractility.

Ivabradine is a pacemaker current or 'funny' current inhibitor that blocks the If ion current present in the sinoatrial node. It can be used as a third agent if angina symptoms are not controlled with the combination of a long-acting dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker and beta-blocker.

Verapamil again can be commenced as a monotherapy calcium-channel blocker in angina but should be avoided with beta-blockers as this can result in significant events including complete heart block.

This patient is already established on the maximum dose of atenolol and therefore titrating up the dose is not an option.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Bleeding risk is assessed with ORBIT, and a high score is not a reason to withhold anticoagulation — it prompts modifying reversible risks. Age and falls risk are explicitly not reasons to withhold it either.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D089 — Cardiology · Heart failure
questions.questionStem: Heart rate 95 beats per minute; irregularly irregular rhythm; absence of P ECG waves
questions.questionHtml:
❓

An 88-year-old man presents with heart palpitations. He has a past medical history of a myocardial infarction and heart failure. His daughter advises you that he has recurrent falls. He takes regular aspirin, ramipril, spironolactone, bisoprolol, and atorvastatin. Observations are as follows: heart rate 95 beats per minute, and blood pressure 155/85 mmHg. An ECG and echocardiogram are performed:

#MRCP #Question

options.text: Echocardiogram No valvular dysfunction. Left ventricular ejection fraction

questions.explanationHtml:
Edoxaban is correct. The ECG features confirm a diagnosis of atrial fibrillation. The patient has a CHA2DS2-VASc score of 5. Therefore anticoagulation is required as a form of stroke prevention. The direct factors Xa inhibitors are now the first line for this purpose (e.g. edoxaban, apixaban or rivaroxaban).

Clopidogrel is incorrect. The patient requires anticoagulation rather than antiplatelet to reduce stroke risk.

Low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) is incorrect. Several studies have shown that treatment with low molecular weight heparin increases the risk of hemorrhagic complications without significantly reducing the rates of stroke in patients with atrial fibrillation. Furthermore, long-term use of LMWH can cause significant complications such as osteoporosis. In addition, daily injections have a negative effect on patients' quality of life. For all these reasons, LMWH is rarely used for long-term stroke prophylaxis.

No treatment indicated is incorrect. Although his older age and recurrent falls will increase his bleeding risk, the significantly elevated CHA2DS2-VASc score confers a significant stroke risk. In these cases, it would be important to counsel the patient with regard to the risks and benefits of anticoagulation. In general, the balance tips towards anticoagulation since the risk of major haemorrhage is relatively low.

Warfarin is incorrect. Warfarin has significant drug-drug, and drug-food interactions, a substantial increase in major haemorrhage (compared to DOACs) [1], and requires intensive monitoring. For all these reasons, warfarin is rarely used for stroke prevention unless the patient has a mechanical heart valve, severe mitral stenosis, or an absolute contraindication to DOACs (e.g. extreme body weight, or drug interaction). Previously warfarin may have been chosen over a DOAC in patients with substantial bleeding risk since warfarin had a highly effective reveal agent (prothrombin complex concentrate). However, DOACs now have a highly effective reversible agent (andexanet alfa) so are usually the agent of choice even in these situations. However, it is important to note that andexanet alfa is only licensed in life- threatening/uncontrolled bleeding for apixaban/rivaroxaban reversal. However, it can be considered off-license for edoxaban reversal. A more important consideration is the fact that warfarin has a much higher rate of spontaneous major haemorrhages (in particular intracerebral) compared to DOACs making DOACs the safer choice in the majority of cases.

References [1] Y. Vinogradova, C. Coupland, T. Hill, J. Hippisley-Cox. Risks and benefits of direct oral anticoagulants versus warfarin in a real world setting: cohort study in primary care. BMJ. 2018; 362

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Four drug classes carry the prognostic benefit in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction:

  • ACE inhibitor (or ARB, or sacubitril-valsartan)
  • Beta-blocker
  • Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist
  • SGLT2 inhibitor

Diuretics sit outside this list — they treat congestion, not mortality.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D090 — Cardiology · Hypertension
questions.questionStem: Which is the most appropriate medication to add next?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 68-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is reviewed in the heart failure clinic. He was recently diagnosed with HFrEF (LVEF 35%) and started on ramipril. He remains breathless on minimal exertion. His renal function is normal.

🩺 Examination:

His blood pressure is 128/78 mmHg and heart rate is 92 bpm in sinus rhythm.

🔬 Investigations:

K+ 4.6 mmol/L (3.5 - 5.0)

Creatinine 98 µmol/L (60 - 110)

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
Bisoprolol is the correct answer. The patient has been diagnosed with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). According to UK guidelines, management should be based on four pillars of therapy: an ACE inhibitor (or ARB/ARNI), a beta-blocker, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (MRA), and an SGLT2 inhibitor. The patient is already on an ACE inhibitor (ramipril). While an MRA and SGLT2 inhibitor are also indicated, the patient's heart rate is elevated at 92 bpm. Initiating a beta- blocker like bisoprolol is the priority here as it will address the tachycardia, which can improve symptoms and diastolic filling, in addition to providing a proven mortality benefit in HFrEF.

  • ❌ Dapagliflozin is one of the four key therapeutic agents for HFrEF and would be a correct addition to this patient's treatment, especially given his type 2 diabetes. However, it does not address the patient's tachycardia. While it should be initiated, the clinical priority in this specific scenario is to control the heart rate with a beta-blocker, which is also a foundational therapy.
  • ❌ Ivabradine is a second-line agent used in HFrEF. It is indicated for patients in sinus rhythm with a heart rate remaining above 75 bpm who are symptomatic despite being on the maximum tolerated dose of a beta-blocker. It would be incorrect to start ivabradine before a beta- blocker has been initiated and up-titrated.
  • ❌ Sacubitril-valsartan is an angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI). It is used as a replacement for an ACE inhibitor or ARB in patients who remain symptomatic despite optimal therapy with an ACEi/ARB, beta-blocker, and MRA. It is not an agent to be added on top of ramipril and is not the next step before other foundational therapies are established.
  • ❌ Spironolactone, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (MRA), is another of the four pillars of HFrEF treatment. The patient's potassium and renal function are suitable for its initiation. However, similar to dapagliflozin, it does not address the tachycardia. Given the heart rate of 92 bpm, initiating a beta-blocker is clinically more pressing.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Treatment targets by age:

  • Under 80 — clinic below 140/90, ABPM/HBPM below 135/85 mmHg
  • 80 and over — clinic below 150/90, ABPM/HBPM below 145/85 mmHg

Out-of-office readings run about 5 mmHg lower than clinic readings, which is where the paired numbers come from.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D091 — Cardiology · Infective endocarditis
questions.questionStem: What should be done next?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 66-year-old man attends his GP surgery for a routine health check. He has no significant past medical history except for mild arthritis of the knee, for which he takes paracetamol.

🩺 Examination:

During the consultation, his blood pressure is noted to be 152/86 mmHg. He is asymptomatic and examination is unremarkable. The blood pressure is repeated and is recorded as 155/82 mmHg.

#MRCP #Question

options.text: Recheck in clinic in one week
Recheck later today with the nurse

questions.explanationHtml:
The correct answer is to arrange ambulatory blood pressure monitoring. Unless the blood pressure is extremely high and requires immediate treatment, NICE now recommends ambulatory or home blood pressure monitoring (ABPM/HBPM), as this provides more reliable readings. In consultation, many patients experience white-coat hypertension and thus have higher-than-normal blood pressure readings. ABPM or HBPM avoids this by allowing the patient's blood pressure to be checked at home, away from the healthcare setting.

Commencing amlodipine is inappropriate - NICE guidelines now recommend confirming a diagnosis of hypertension with ABPM/HBPM first.

Similarly, commencing ramipril would be inappropriate. Furthermore, ramipril would be used in patients under 55 and not of African/Caribbean descent - if this patient were to start treatment now, amlodipine would be more appropriate.

Arranging for the patient to come back in one week for a recheck is not ideal - the same problem may occur with regards to white-coat hypertension. ABPM would be preferable to this.

Rechecking again now would serve no purpose if the patient were experiencing white-coat hypertension.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Antibiotic prophylaxis against infective endocarditis is not routinely recommended for people undergoing dental procedures in the UK — a position that remains out of step with European and American guidance.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D092 — Cardiology · Supraventricular tachycardia
questions.questionStem: What antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended prior to this procedure?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 72-year-old woman is due to have a tooth extracted next week. Her past medical history is significant for an aortic valve replacement 2 years previously.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
General oral hygiene advice is correct. NICE guidance from 2008 recommended that patients undergoing dental procedures are not routinely offered infective endocarditis prophylaxis. This includes those deemed 'at risk' due to cardiac conditions such as valve replacement or structural heart disease.

Chlorhexidine mouthwash is incorrect. The BNF page 'antibacterials, use for prophylaxis' states that chlorhexidine mouthwash is not recommended for the prevention of infective endocarditis.

Intravenous co-amoxiclav, oral amoxicillin and oral phenoxymethylpenicillin are all incorrect. NICE does not routinely recommend antibiotics before dental procedures as infective endocarditis prophylaxis. This is because there is no clear association between dental procedures and infective endocarditis. Antibiotic prophylaxis, therefore, exposes patients to side effects without evidence substantiating their use.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Adenosine is diagnostic as well as therapeutic in a regular narrow-complex tachycardia — but in a broad-complex tachycardia of uncertain origin, verapamil is contraindicated, since giving it to ventricular tachycardia can precipitate cardiovascular collapse.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D093 — Cardiology · Acute coronary syndrome
questions.questionStem: Which one of the following statements is true regarding this man’s tachycardia?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 20-year-old-man attends the Emergency Department with palpitations described as ‘regular rapid beating of the heart’. The tachycardia spontaneously resolves. An ECG in sinus rhythm reveals a PR interval of 60 ms and a QRS duration of 120 ms, with a positive delta in V1.

🔬 Investigations:

An ECG shows a regular rhythm with a rate of 200 bpm and a QRS duration of 80 ms.

#MRCP #Question

options.text: Carotid sinus massage will be ineffective
Intravenous adenosine is of no use
Digoxin should be used as a prophylactic agent
Atrial fibrillation is well tolerated in such patients

questions.explanationHtml:
Verapamil is contraindicated as it increases conduction in the bypass tract; this increases the risk of rapid conduction of an atrial arrhythmia along the accessory pathway and potential ventricular arrhythmias.

This man has type A Wolff–Parkinson–White (WPW) syndrome, in which an abnormal band of atrial tissue connects the atria to the ventricle, bypassing the atrioventricular (AV) node.

As the AV node and bypass tract have different conduction speeds and refractory periods, a re-entry circuit can be formed that results in tachycardia.

WPW patients typically have a shortened PR interval, and have a delta wave with prolongation of the QRS complex.

Prophylactic drug therapy is indicated for symptomatic patients. Agents used in an attempt to slow the conduction rate and prolong the refractory period of the bypass tract are:

flecainide

procainamide ibutilide amiodarone.

  • ❌ A. Carotid sinus massage will be ineffective — Carotid sinus massage will often terminate an episode of tachycardia.
  • ❌ B. Intravenous adenosine is of no use — Intravenous adenosine will often terminate an episode of tachycardia. Adenosine is usually avoided because of the risk of precipitating VF in a small percentage of patients with WPW; this occurs predominantly in patients with an accessory pathway and atrial fibrillation or another atrial arrhythmia. Giving adenosine may selectively block the AV node but not the accessory pathway since this lacks the rate-limiting properties of the AV node. This would allow rapid conduction of the atrial arrhythmia along the accessory pathway; this could trigger ventricular fibrillation.
  • ❌ C. Digoxin should be used as a prophylactic agent — Digoxin is contraindicated as it increases conduction in the bypass tract; this increases the risk of rapid conduction of an atrial arrhythmia along the accessory pathway and potential ventricular arrhythmias.
  • ❌ E. Atrial fibrillation is well tolerated in such patients — Atrial fibrillation is well tolerated in such patients is incorrect. The presence of AF in patients with WPW should be treated as a medical emergency with DC cardioversion.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Dual antiplatelet therapy continues for up to 12 months after myocardial infarction, then aspirin alone indefinitely — unless there is a separate indication for anticoagulation.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D094 — Cardiology · Aortic stenosis
questions.questionStem: Which one of the following factors should determine if an intravenous glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor antagonist is to be given?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 55-year-old man is admitted with central chest pain. Past medical history includes a thrombolysed myocardial infarction 2 years ago, asthma and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Treatment with aspirin, clopidogrel and unfractionated heparin is commenced.

🔬 Investigations:

His ECG shows ST depression in the inferior leads and the chest pain requires intravenous morphine to settle.

#MRCP #Question

options.text: High GRACE (Global Registry of Acute Cardiac Events) risk score + whether a percutaneous coronary intervention is to be performed
High GRACE (Global Registry of Acute Cardiac Events) risk score
Presence of a left ventricular thrombus
The presence of recurrent cardiac chest pain

questions.correctAnswerText: High GRACE (Global Registry of Acute Cardiac Events) risk score + whether a percutaneous coronary intervention is to be performed
questions.explanationHtml:
The correct answer is High GRACE (Global Registry of Acute Cardiac Events) risk score + whether a percutaneous coronary intervention is to be performed. The use of intravenous glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor antagonists, such as abciximab, eptifibatide, or tirofiban, is determined by the patient's GRACE risk score and whether they are undergoing a percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). According to UK guidelines, these agents can be considered for high-risk patients with non-ST elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) when PCI is planned within 96 hours of hospital admission.

The option Degree of ST depression is incorrect because the degree of ST depression on an ECG does not directly determine the use of glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor antagonists. However, it may contribute to the overall assessment of a patient's risk and management plan.

High GRACE (Global Registry of Acute Cardiac Events) risk score alone is not sufficient to determine if an intravenous glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor antagonist should be given. As mentioned earlier, both the high GRACE risk score and planned PCI within 96 hours are required for considering these agents in NSTEMI patients.

The presence of a left ventricular thrombus does not directly influence the decision to administer glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor antagonists. Left ventricular thrombus formation typically occurs after an ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) rather than NSTEMI and may require anticoagulation therapy with warfarin or direct oral anticoagulants.

Finally, the presence of recurrent cardiac chest pain does not solely dictate the use of intravenous glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor antagonists. While recurrent chest pain may indicate ongoing myocardial ischemia, the decision to use these agents depends on the GRACE risk score and planned PCI, as discussed earlier.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Low-gradient aortic stenosis with an ejection fraction below 50% needs dobutamine stress echocardiography — a weak ventricle cannot generate a high gradient, so the gradient alone understates severity.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D095 — Cardiology · Angina pectoris
questions.questionStem: Which one of the following clinical signs would best indicate severe aortic stenosis?

options.text: Valvular gradient of less than 30 mmHg
Carotid radiation of ejection systolic murmur

questions.explanationHtml:
The correct answer is Soft second heart sound. In severe aortic stenosis, the second heart sound (A2) becomes soft or absent due to the reduced mobility and increased calcification of the aortic valve cusps. This reduces the intensity of the aortic component of S2, making it a reliable clinical indicator of severe stenosis. The softening of A2 correlates well with disease severity and is a key finding during cardiac auscultation.

  • ❌ Valvular gradient of less than 30 mmHg is incorrect because severe aortic stenosis is characterised by a high pressure gradient across the valve, typically greater than 40 mmHg. A gradient less than 30 mmHg would suggest mild stenosis or could indicate low-flow, low-gradient aortic stenosis in the context of poor left ventricular function.
  • ❌ Quiet first heart sound is incorrect because the first heart sound is typically normal in aortic stenosis. S1 is produced by mitral and tricuspid valve closure and is not significantly affected by aortic valve pathology.
  • ❌ Development of an opening snap is incorrect because opening snaps are characteristic of mitral stenosis, not aortic stenosis. The opening snap occurs just after S2 and represents the sudden opening of a stenotic mitral valve. It is never present in isolated aortic stenosis.
  • ❌ Carotid radiation of ejection systolic murmur is incorrect as a specific indicator of severe stenosis because whilst radiation to the carotids is typical of aortic stenosis, it occurs in both mild and severe cases. The radiation pattern alone cannot differentiate the severity of stenosis. Other characteristics such as timing, duration, and intensity of the murmur are more reliable indicators of severity.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

If both a beta-blocker and a calcium channel blocker are contraindicated or not tolerated, use monotherapy with a long-acting nitrate, ivabradine, nicorandil or ranolazine — these are never first-line.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D096 — Cardiology · Atrial fibrillation
questions.questionStem: What medication should be added to improve his symptoms?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 60-year-old man is referred to the cardiology clinic with recurrent exertional chest pain associated with dyspnoea. It improves with rest. He has a history of ischaemic heart disease and underwent PCI to the right coronary artery five years ago. A coronary angiogram six weeks ago showed widely patent stents. His current medications include aspirin, ramipril, bisoprolol, eplerenone, and atorvastatin. Recently, his GP started him on sildenafil for erectile dysfunction.

🩺 Examination:

On assessment, his BP is 142/88 mmHg, and his heart rate is 70 bpm.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
Modified-release nifedipine is a long-acting dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (CCB) that can be used in combination with beta- blockers for the management of angina. If symptoms persist following the addition of a CCB, then a third agent can be added. Options include isosorbide mononitrate, ivabradine, nicorandil, or ranolazine.

  • ❌ Atenolol is a beta blocker that may be considered in the treatment of angina. However, bisoprolol is more cardio-selective and is currently the first choice beta blocker for the management of angina and heart failure. Moreover, adding a second beta-blocker is not recommended as it can cause severe hypotension/bradycardia.
  • ❌ Isosorbide mononitrate is a long-acting nitrate that relieves angina by causing coronary vasodilation. It may be considered in the management of angina pectoris after the addition of a calcium channel blocker; however, concomitant use of nitrates and PDE5 inhibitors like sildenafil is contraindicated as it can cause severe refractory hypotension.
  • ❌ Nicorandil is a nitrous oxide donor and potassium channel opener that causes coronary vasodilation. Hence it may be considered in the management of angina but only after the addition of a calcium channel blocker. Also, the concurrent use of nicorandil and PDE5 inhibitors is contraindicated as it can cause severe refractory hypotension.
  • ❌ Verapamil is a rate-limiting calcium channel blocker that may be used as first-line monotherapy for angina when beta blockers are not tolerated or contraindicated. However, when the patient is already receiving beta blockers, the addition of verapamil is not recommended as it can cause dangerous bradyarrhythmias, including complete heart block.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Rate control is the first-line strategy for most patients — the exceptions being a reversible cause, heart failure thought to be caused by the AF, new-onset AF, or atrial flutter suitable for ablation.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D097 — Cardiology · Heart failure
questions.questionStem: Which option is the best next step?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 32-year-old man has 3 months of episodic palpitations without chest pain or syncope. He has no history of hypertension, diabetes, or ischaemic heart disease. The left ventricle and heart valves are normal on echocardiography. He is first treated with flecainide, but remains symptomatic. Following this, electrical cardioversion is attempted, which is unsuccessful. He has also trialled bisoprolol without success.

🩺 Examination:

Lung sounds are clear, and he has no peripheral oedema.

🔬 Investigations:

An ECG shows an irregularly irregular rhythm with absent P-waves at a rate of 130 bpm.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
Refer for radiofrequency ablation is correct. This patient's likely diagnosis is symptomatic persistent atrial fibrillation, evidenced by a 3- month history of episodic palpitations, an irregularly irregular pulse of 130 bpm, and absent P-waves on ECG. This patient remains symptomatic despite flecainide, electrical cardioversion, and bisoprolol, a beta-blocker. He has no contraindications to ablation, such as structural heart disease or heart failure, making him an ideal candidate. NICE guidelines recommend catheter ablation for patients who fail or wish to avoid antiarrhythmic drugs, offering better long-term rhythm control and symptom relief than switching to amiodarone, which carries significant toxicity risks.

  • ❌ Refer for electrical cardioversion is incorrect, as this patient has already undergone unsuccessful electrical cardioversion, indicating that further attempts are unlikely to restore or maintain sinus rhythm. Electrical cardioversion is most relevant in patients with new-onset atrial fibrillation (< 48 hours) or those haemodynamically unstable, neither of which applies here. While electrical cardioversion can acutely restore sinus rhythm, its effectiveness diminishes in persistent AF lasting over 48 hours without prior anticoagulation and in cases refractory to initial attempts, as seen in this patient.
  • ❌ Switch to amiodarone is incorrect. This patient is relatively young, has no structural heart disease, and has not yet tried catheter ablation, which is preferred due to better safety and efficacy for maintaining sinus rhythm. Amiodarone is generally considered for patients with coexisting heart failure or those who have failed or are unsuitable for ablation. While it can maintain sinus rhythm, its significant long-term toxicities, including pulmonary fibrosis and thyroid dysfunction, make it less favourable in young patients without heart failure, as seen here.
  • ❌ Switch to digoxin is incorrect, as this patient is young and likely physically active. Digoxin is less effective at controlling heart rate during exercise, and is often considered for rate control in patients who do little or no physical activity or have coexistent heart failure; neither applies here, as the patient has normal left ventricular function and no heart failure signs. Since this patient has attempted pharmacological and electrical rhythm control, and rate control with bisoprolol, the best next step is referring for catheter ablation.
  • ❌ Switch to sotalol is incorrect. This patient has already tried flecainide without success and remains symptomatic; sotalol, a class III antiarrhythmic with beta-blocking properties, carries risks of proarrhythmia and requires careful monitoring, making it less favourable as a next step before considering catheter ablation. While sotalol may be considered in patients with paroxysmal AF who have failed first-line agents and no significant QT prolongation or structural heart disease, this patient’s persistent symptoms despite flecainide and cardioversion suggest that ablation offers a more effective and definitive treatment.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

A beta-blocker is continued indefinitely after myocardial infarction when the ejection fraction is reduced. With a preserved ejection fraction, 12 months is considered, and continuing beyond that is a discussion, not a rule.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D098 — Cardiology · Hypertension
questions.questionStem: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 68-year-old man with heart failure attends cardiology clinic for review. He was diagnosed 18 months ago with left ventricular systolic dysfunction following an anterior myocardial infarction. Despite optimal titration of ramipril, bisoprolol, spironolactone and dapagliflozin, he remains breathless on minimal exertion. Echocardiography shows left ventricular ejection fraction of 28%.

🩺 Examination:

His blood pressure is 118/76 mmHg and heart rate 68 bpm.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
Switch ramipril to sacubitril-valsartan is correct. This patient has heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and remains symptomatic despite being on optimal doses of 'the big 4' medications (ACE-inhibitor, beta- blocker, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, and SGLT2-inhibitor). According to NICE 2025 guidelines, the next step is to switch the ACE- inhibitor to an angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI) such as sacubitril-valsartan. This should be done in consultation with a heart failure specialist. ARNIs have been shown to reduce cardiovascular mortality and heart failure hospitalisations compared to ACE-inhibitors alone in patients who remain symptomatic on standard therapy.

  • ❌ Add ivabradine would be considered second-line specialist therapy, but the patient does not meet the criteria as his heart rate is 68 bpm. Ivabradine is indicated when the heart rate is greater than 75 bpm in sinus rhythm with left ventricular ejection fraction below 35%. This patient's heart rate is already well-controlled on bisoprolol.
  • ❌ Add digoxin is a second-line treatment that may improve symptoms but has not been shown to reduce mortality. It would be considered after switching to an ARNI, or if the patient had coexistent atrial fibrillation requiring rate control.
  • ❌ Add hydralazine with isosorbide dinitrate is second-line therapy that may be particularly beneficial in Afro-Caribbean patients. However, switching to an ARNI takes priority in patients symptomatic on the four first-line medications.
  • ❌ Increase spironolactone dose is not appropriate as the question states he is on optimal titration of all four first-line medications, implying maximum tolerated doses have been achieved.

#MRCP #Answer
questions.pearlHtml:
💡

Clinic blood pressure of 180/120 mmHg or higher with retinal haemorrhage, papilloedema, or life-threatening symptoms requires same-day specialist review — otherwise start treatment immediately and repeat clinic measurement within 7 days.

#MRCP #Pearl

questions.name: D099 — Cardiology · Infective endocarditis
questions.questionStem: Which one of the following agents would be the most appropriate immediate management?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 39-year-old female is admitted with pulmonary oedema, blood pressure 195/134 mmHg and fundoscopy showing retinal haemorrhages but not papilloedema. She has systemic sclerosis and asthma.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
Malignant hypertension is a rare condition characterised by very high blood pressures, with bilateral retinal haemorrhages and/or exudates or cotton wool spots, without the added requirement for papilloedema.

All patients with malignant hypertension should be admitted for assessment, investigation and commencement of therapy under supervision. Malignant hypertension may be associated with hypertensive crises including LVF with pulmonary oedema, myocardial infarction (MI) and encephalopathy. In these patients rapid but controlled lowering of BP with intra-arterial BP monitoring on the ICU is indicated – aiming for a diastolic reduction of 10– 15% (or to 110 mmHg) within 1 h. A titratable IV agent is ideal, such as sodium nitroprusside

  • ❌ A. Atenolol — Atenolol is incorrect. In patients without hypertensive crises, the initial aim of treatment is to lower the diastolic pressure to about 100–105 mmHg over a period of 2–3 days, with oral therapy where possible and dose escalation at daily intervals if necessary. A ß-blocker (such as atenolol) may be used for this purpose; however, this patient needs more urgent IV treatment (and β-blockers would be contra-indicated here regardless due to asthma).
  • ❌ B. Intravenous labetalol — Intravenous labetalol is incorrect. Labetalol is an excellent agent for urgent treatment of hypertensive crises, and has a less toxic profile and easier handling than sodium nitroprusside. However, it would be prudent to avoid β-blockade in this asthmatic patient. Cardio selective beta blockers are at low risk to precipitate asthma exacerbation.
  • ❌ D. Nifedipine oral — Nifedipine oral is incorrect. Both oral and sublingual nifedipine have been shown to precipitate sudden and severe blood pressure reductions associated with cerebral, renal and myocardial events, sometimes with devastating outcomes. Their use is therefore no longer recommended for malignant hypertension.
  • ❌ E. Nifedipine sublingual — Nifedipine sublingual is incorrect. Both oral and sublingual nifedipine have been shown to precipitate sudden and severe blood pressure reductions associated with cerebral, renal and myocardial events, sometimes with devastating outcomes. Their use is therefore no longer recommended for malignant hypertension.

  • Imaging — echocardiographic evidence of vegetation, abscess, pseudoaneurysm, or new dehiscence of a prosthetic valve

questions.name: D100 — Cardiology · Supraventricular tachycardia
questions.questionStem: Given the likely diagnosis, which one of the following is an indication for surgery in this patient?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 62-year-old man is admitted to the hospital with a 10-day history of feeling generally unwell with malaise and weight loss. His past medical history includes childhood rheumatic fever.

🩺 Examination:

On examination, he is febrile and there is an audible pansystolic heart murmur, loudest over the mitral area and radiating to the axilla. He has mild peripheral oedema up to his ankles.

🔬 Investigations:

Electrocardiogram: heart rate 50 bpm, QRS 110 ms, PR interval 210 ms. Blood cultures are taken and he is started on intravenous antibiotics.

Investigation Result Normal value

Haemoglobin (Hb) 108 g/l 135–175 g/l

White cell count (WCC) 11.2 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l

Platelets 153 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l

C-reactive protein (CRP) 162 mg/l 0–10 mg/l

Sodium (Na +) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l

Potassium (K +) 4.2 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l

Creatinine 156 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l

#MRCP #Question

options.text: Isolated Staphylococcus aureus from blood culture

questions.explanationHtml:
This patient has infective endocarditis (IE), given the history of fever, malaise and the presence of an audible murmur against a background of rheumatic heart disease. The description of the murmur is typical for mitral regurgitation which may have occurred post-rheumatic fever. An electrocardiogram finding of PR interval prolongation suggests the presence of paravalvular extension of the infection (paravalvular abscess/myocardial abscess), which is an indication of surgery in the case of IE.

  • ❌ A. CRP > 100 mg/l — C-reactive protein is an indicator of infection or inflammation, rather than an indication of a requirement for surgery in endocarditis. C-reactive protein level will be elevated due to the infection and can be elevated due to inflammation and end-organ damage of embolic events. The levels of other acute-phase reaction proteins will also be elevated secondary to infective endocarditis (IE). They can, however, be elevated with an alternative diagnosis such as vasculitis.
  • ❌ B. Isolated Staphylococcus aureus from blood culture — Infections that are resistant to standard treatment with intravenous antibiotics are an indication for surgical intervention; however, surgery is not based on the presence of a particular organism. Blood cultures positive for Staphylococcus aureus should raise the possibility of seeding to heart valves and intervertebral discs. Three sets of blood cultures should be taken in patients suspected of IE, before therapy commences.
  • ❌ C. Peripheral oedema — An indication for surgery in IE includes cardiac failure refractory to standard medical treatment. This patient has mild peripheral oedema, with no evidence to suggest pulmonary overload. Given that this patient has not been initiated on any medical treatment for cardiac failure, opting for surgical intervention would be too premature at this stage.
  • ❌ D. Persistent murmur — Murmurs often do not significantly improve with treatment of endocarditis; hence, a persistent murmur is not an indication for surgery. However, severe valve dysfunction, invasion of infection beyond the valve leaflets or a prosthetic valve would lead to consideration of early surgical intervention. Endocarditis initially starts along the edges of the valve, before leading to ulceration, erosion and eventual perforation of the valve leaflet. This leads to incompetence and regurgitation of blood across the valve.

questions.name: D101 — Cardiology · Supraventricular tachycardia (answer only)
questions.questionStem: What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.questionHtml:
❓

A 30-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department following the acute onset of palpitations. Intravenous access is gained and 6mg of adenosine is given with no effect.

🩺 Examination:

Blood pressure is 124/84 mmHg and her pulse is 150/min.

🔬 Investigations:

An ECG shows a narrow complex tachycardia.

#MRCP #Question
questions.explanationHtml:
The correct answer is Intravenous adenosine 12 mg. In the management of supraventricular tachycardia (SVT), which presents as a narrow complex tachycardia, the first-line treatment is adenosine. According to UK guidelines, the initial dose is 6mg given as a rapid bolus. If this is unsuccessful, the next step is to give a higher dose of 12mg adenosine. This approach is recommended because adenosine has an extremely short half-life (less than 10 seconds), is relatively safe, and can be both diagnostic and therapeutic.

  • ❌ Intravenous adenosine 6mg would be incorrect as this dose has already been tried and failed. Repeating the same dose would be unlikely to achieve success when it has already proven ineffective.
  • ❌ Intravenous verapamil 2.5-5 mg would be inappropriate at this stage. While calcium channel blockers can be effective in treating SVT, they are typically considered after adenosine has failed at maximum doses. Additionally, verapamil has a longer half-life and more potential side effects than adenosine.
  • ❌ Radio-frequency ablation is incorrect as this is a long-term management strategy for recurrent SVT, not an acute intervention. It requires careful planning, electrophysiology studies, and is performed in a specialist setting.
  • ❌ Electrical cardioversion would be inappropriate at this stage as it is reserved for haemodynamically unstable patients or when pharmacological interventions have failed. This patient is haemodynamically stable (normal blood pressure) and has not yet exhausted medical management options.
